There's always the worry with these kinds of games that they will be too boring, hard or pretentious. Not that I consider myself stupid (who does though) or unwilling to engage with "intellectual" media but I cannot say that I have much patience for it either. To my surprise I found Pathologic 2 to be... much milder than expected. That's not to say that it's easy or perfect. The game always has hard choices for you to make and it can frustrate and at times it can even feel a bit cheap in its writing (or in other departments). Though it will make it hard on you, it will never leave you alone either.

This is not a 100% front to back literary masterpiece but I think it gets pretty close to what I imagine "high art" video games to be, a solid 80%. It's strangeness rarely feels "random", it's eerie but it doesn't try to say "look how crazy this world is, it's it weird?" And it has a lot of (melancholic) charm to it as well, especially the children which are typically not the greatest part of video games. There's definitely humanity in it. What I also like is the real tension. I'm 5 days in and I'm genuinely afraid I'll fuck this up.

I've heard people say it's fun to discuss but not to play but frankly I'd rather experience it than sit here and write about it. I recommend Pathologic 2, just don't go in and expect it to a) be easy and b) be the greatest experience you've ever had.

This game is heavily praised for its writing, but I believe its gameplay far outshines its plot and characters. This game is hard. You'll be digging through dumpsters and trashcans to find scraps to barter for food and medical items all while time ticks away at your hunger, your thirst, your exhaustion, and the lives of the patients you must save. Time is as much the enemy as the plague that ravages the Town. Many times during my playthrough I felt a sense of hopelessness and desperation I haven't felt in any other game as I was forced to choose which patients I could treat with my dwindling resources before the precious minutes separating that day and the next ticked away and sealed their fates.

In terms of writing, Pathologic 2 is... shaky. The plot is certainly interesting, as you return an outsider to a Town split between modernity and tradition in order to save it and its strange, divided population from the plague. Left by your late father is a list of important figures in the Town for whom you must do your best to keep alive. Most of the writing in Pathologic 2 is contained within dialogues between you and these characters, so you would expect them to all be well-written. 

However, despite quantity of words spent on these characters, there were only a handful of characters that I truly cared about and wanted to keep alive ("Care" meaning sympathy as well as interest in those who were unsympathetic yet well-written). Some characters seem to serve as lore dumps, others skate on "this character is a child, therefore you automatically care for them no matter how little substance they have," and some you barely even speak to. Pathologic expects me to care about these characters because they're on my father's list, but in reality, I couldn't care less about half the cast dying

However, for those characters that were given arcs and personalities, that I loved or hated, I fought as hard as I could to keep them alive so I could see where their stories ended. That's where Pathologic 2 shines, where its gameplay seamlessly connects with its story, making you feel as if these characters are your patients rather than gameplay objectives. Despite its flaws, Pathologic 2 is an amazing game, and I recommend it to anyone looking for a piece of art that will affect them like no other.

Pathologic 2 is kinda hard to describe. It's a very bizarre open world survival horror game about a small town being ravaged by plague. You're a doctor and you have to figure out what's causing the plague and how to create a cure, all the while being stalked by people and unknown entities. Similar to Dead Rising's time cap, you have 12 days to complete the game, which is around 25-30 hours. 

The town and it's people feel like they belong in another reality, in an uncanny valley sort of way. The atmosphere is filled with dread and hopelessness. From the moment the game begins, the town seems like Purgatory. The whole town will slowly start to become insane and men won't be above murder for long. Sound design and music are top notch. Voice acting is limited, but it's understandable because there's tons and tons of dialogue. It has an insane amount of interesting lore in it. The writing is absolutely unforgettably phenomenal. You boot the game up and you're immediately immersed in this weird, dark, terrifying world. 

For a long time, you'll probably end up having absolutely no idea what the hell is going on, and most characters seem to be speaking in riddles! And if you ask them about what's going on, they seem to have no clue either. NPC's can lie here. Unlike in most RPG's, you can't trust people face-up. They have their own agendas and world views. If you believe everything that every NPC you meet says, you'll end up getting screwed over.

Gameplay itself is nothing special, but it's by no means bad in any way. Basic FPS controls with looting and sneaking. Melee combat and shooting is fine, although I have to say, any kind combat in this game is like a dizzying nightmare. You'll be horrified to know that a fight is about to start. Killing and dying is fast, the combat in general is vicious and uncertain. Dying is the last thing you ever want to happen. If you're anything like me, you'll probably do everything in your capabilities to avoid a fight of any kind.

The game as a whole is like one massive puzzle which you will most likely not figure out the first time playing, and you'll probably end up starting over, which I think is intended. You're supposed to learn from your past mistakes and try again. The game is absolutely brutal and making big mistakes can easily lead to having to start over. But things become manageable once you understand what is required of you. It doesn't require complex pattern recognition or lightning fast reflexes, quite the contrary, the game is slow in terms of combat and survival mechanics. It's all about carefully planning ahead and thinking for yourself.

I love the description on the store page, it sums up the difficulty pretty well: "An uphill battle. Your own body is only waiting for an opportunity to give up and betray you. Things are changing from bad to worse and the odds are stacked against you."

I highly recommend this masterpiece if you're willing to test your sanity and patience. There's nothing quite like it. Pathologic 2 blew my mind, it's easily one of the most engaging and unforgettable experiences in entertainment I've ever had. With that said, it's definitely not for everyone. It's not a fun game at all and it isn't trying to be, it's an experience. Many times I felt needlessly tormented and stressed out about things like whether or not I am going to make it somewhere in time, or if I am going to run out of supplies, and if I do, what depravities would I  have to do to get myself back on track. But the reward of seeing more incredible dialogue and lore and seeing where everything is going was always way more than enough to keep me going. In many ways it even gives everything it's distinct flavor; you're suffering just like the rest of the Town is. 

I guess Pathologic 2 even made me kind of obsessed about it for a few weeks. Not sure if there will ever be anything like it again, but it's definitely altered my view of art and entertainment in general. It's by no means the timeless Holy Grail, but if we ever get to see the perfect piece of entertainment, it's on these tracks.

I find this game extremely difficult, I cannot play it for too long in one sitting. Due to my own personal mix of traumas and mental health issues, this game is emotionally taxing to power on through. I am perpetually afraid of making the tinest mistake, I am perpetually filled with dread over what is next to come. It is punishing, too: If you die, it will make it permanently harder to play the game.

It is also an incredible game that I think everyone should give a go at least once. You do not need to have played the first game to understand this. In fact, I would go so far as to specifically recommend that you avoid the first game and any spoilers related to it. Your experience with the game will be better for it. This game makes you care about people by placing you and them under hardship. The game will immerse you through hardship. Without that hardship, it would simply be a game about wandering from place to place in an odd town. Instead, it is a game about survival, about failure, about misery, about the deaths of those in your care, about progress vs tradition, about idealism vs realism, about plague and Utopia.

It's good. But it's very heavy, it's very difficult, it's frustrating, it's harrowing, it's dense, it's gruelling... and that's the point. It is not a pleasant experience, but it is a powerful one. I hate it. It's incredible. Play it. It's good. Extremely good.

If you're like me you have known about Pathologic for some time, but have been too intimidated to play it. Before starting it in earnest this game sat gathering dust in my library for over two years because I started it up, bumbled through the bizarre tutorial and starved to death on day 2. Uninstall!
I'll say this up front: If you have the disposable income available, buy this game. Buy it even if you never intend on playing it. The people who made it deserve to get paid and it would be a tragedy if these genuine genius visionaries weren't allowed to make another game because its not *profitable*.
Trying to describe the game is a fool's errand for a couple reasons. First, it is genuinely unique. Of the hundreds of games I've played over the years none of them were like Pathologic, making it hard to describe using gamerspeak. Second, and more importantly, discovering the intricacies of the game's systems is a large part of the fun. That being said I'm gonna briefly describe it anyway because I'm a moron. The game is essentially a pandemic response simulation with strict survival mechanics.
If ever there was a game whose reputation preceded itself it would be Pathologic. If you've heard of this game you've heard that its extremely weird, difficult, and buggy. It is most certainly the first (which is a plus if you aren't a square), but is it really as hard as its cracked up to be... Yes? Kind of. I am on the game's fifth day of twelve and I have died over a dozen times. There is no doubt that it is hard, but what makes this game special is that, in order to succeed on its default difficulty, you must be tuned in. You can't float through it like you can most games, every decision made has benefits and drawbacks that have vast ripple effects thanks to the games tightly interwoven systems. While this can be frustrating, it also makes the game engaging like nothing else. The joy and relief that filled my heart when I found an idiot child that would trade me morphine, immunity boosters, and an egg for a handful of peanuts rivals anything I've felt in games infinitely more flashy. To sum up, yes, the game is super fucking hard, but in a way that beautifully evokes in the player the same desperation felt by its protagonist and makes it nearly impossible to be bored.
Surprisingly i haven't run across any game breaking bugs. The game runs like ass and NPC voice lines will sometimes repeat  over and over, but it hasn't crashed and I haven't lost any items or progress to bugs. The games most obvious weakness is its combat. It sucks, and not in a *thematically appropriate* way either. I don't think it should have been removed because the threat of being shanked adds an exciting wrinkle to looting post-infection areas of the city, but feedback on punches is really bad. Perhaps this could have been mitigated by making stealth more engaging and functional? Whatever, i'm not a game developer, and combat is a minuscule slice of pemmican in this tasty pie.

If you’re ready for an unforgettable and harrowing journey, Pathologic 2 will stay with you long after the credits roll.

Not only is the story and general atmosphere incredibly interesting, having to survive in the world of Pathologic is incredibly engaging and extremely fun. The close-range combat is not my favorite part, but successfully getting a hit in on an enemy and taking their stuff means that I'm willing to take it for how it is.
On another note, the trading system is incredibly simple, but I've never seen any other game do it quite like this. Store-owners are the only NPCs that take money, and they're locked inside their establishment, while regular people roam the streets. Vendors are pretty scarce on the map, and you have an extremely limited amount of time to do things during the day, so you don't wanna make huge detours unless it's necessary. Regular civilians will trade in items, and every one of them has their own preferences, so while in my current playthrough I have a bit of money, I'm barely managing to get by on the slim amounts of food and healing items I can obtain.
What little jank there is I am able to look over due to the immense amount of enjoyment I've already gotten out of it.
The atmosphere and story go hand-in-hand, and both are unlike any other game I've played before. I tried the first game, and found it to be far too difficult and complicated for me to actually get into. This, however, I am more than able to get into. The music is tinny and weird, the way characters act and talk is bizarre, and I've realized that I become extremely nervous and greedy when playing it. 
A good example of this is that I was originally hoarding money for a particularly expensive item, but recently I decided not to buy it. So if I'm not in need of the money for the expensive item, why am I still insistent on hoarding it? I need food and various other things to keep me alive, but I'm still looking to make a profit when it's not that important. I should just buy food and supplies, but I'm not. 
On another note, due to an early rep-hit, I'm now constantly looking over my shoulder and worried about someone chasing me even though my reputation is positive everywhere. The enemies that only appear at night are not helping my paranoia.
It's so good at what it does that it makes me fall back on self-destructive and neurotic tendencies in-game. Hopefully the devs keep making stuff, 'cause they're extremely talented and I want to see more of whatever ideas they come up with. 10/10.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

i'm going to share a personal story on why I'm recommending Pathologic 2.

Back in 2016, I read the RPS review of Pathologic 1, right before I went on a trip to Wales for a week away from my PC. I'd also just updated my playlist with a few tracks meant to freshen up the long car journey there and back, one of which was titled "Ghosts", the other "Way Back Home". Neither is anything like the music in either game, but they still conjured up images of what I'd read in the RPS review, and what ensued was a full week of daydreaming about this mythical game, building up an almost impossible expectation in my head for it. I came home at the end of the week, bought the game, and immediately began playing it. What I was met with was a jankfest that wasn't very fun to play, and not for the "right" reasons. I persevered anyway, but when I got the worst possible ending, I concluded that I'd built up a game in my head that didn't exist, and gave up.

Then I played Pathologic 2. Pathologic 2 is that game I daydreamed about for a full week. Pathologic 2 is that blend of survival and bleakness with solid art direction and execution. Pathologic 2 is challenging to play for the RIGHT reasons. The singular thing the original has over Pathologic 2 is that all three character storylines are done and playable, and with this game's apparent failure commercially, the sequel may never have the same. But just the Haruspex storyline is so compelling in this game, so tightly executed, that I would still, unflinchingly, recommend it.

It's amazing. I am only on Day 5 (there is 12) as of writing, but it's fantastic.
The atmosphere and noises are perfect, although in the first few days some didn't make much sense (you hear wailing a lot, but in the first few days there is no pandemic so it was a bit confusing). Afterwards though, it was brilliant. 
I try to limit my spoilers, I only looked up what some mechanics were because it was confusing me (and I am the type of person who likes understanding mechanics). The story has been unspoiled though and I intend to keep it that way until the end. 
I play on the "Intended" difficulty, but it's nice that they included easier options and customisability for those that struggle with games. So far, on Day 5, I can see the game ramping up in difficulty, and I'm most not looking forward to [spoiler]the water gradually turning off and having to be fixed.[/spoiler] This is great though, as it keeps you tense. 
I don't think it is impossibly hard, I actually think sleeping and eating mechanics are fairly lenient (although it does sting having to sleep and not having time to do things, but that is part of the game and story). 
I'm not sure how I feel about [spoiler] children's caches [/spoiler] as I feel it hinges too much on you being forced to remember where they all are, and I have been tempted to just google where the rare ones are each day. 

Also, I must say, I wrote this out and posted it and then realised I forgot this. The writing is fantastic. For Russian developers, it is incredibly well-written in English. Really surprisingly so. The story is great, and at first you will be confused, you won't understand anything. This is intentional, you will gradually begin picking up on the world and understanding it as the game progresses (if you read the dialogue, anyway). It is even immersive in that aspect as you are given choices a lot of the time to say "I know this" or "I have no idea what you are talking about" and that changes their response. This is such an excellent feature for repeat playthroughs or just anyone getting into the game who may have played the others or watched a video or anything. I've not seen this utilised in any other game, it is so simple and yet so immersive. 

I usually review AFTER completing a game, but this one is just fantastic, and a great length too. 

Only issues: The performance was awful at first, I believe because of the Unity Engine. There was a fix for this that worked for me though:  https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2847169669
This literally boosted my GPU usage from 50% to 100% and I had +100fps more. 
The other is that I believe they said the Bachelor story (the original game had 3 stories/characters) is coming "in the foreseeable future..." back in 2020. I understand COVID and everything occurred, but with the map already being built and everything, 3 years for another story (and still seemingly no sight of it being near) is very long. The base game and story is fantastic on its own though. It'll be nice to replay as the Bachelor story when it does come out, as well as the Changeling after that.  
All of that said, it seems the studio fell on fairly hard times (https://teletype.in/@icepicklodge/QC8lkECDPqZ), they also appear to want the two next stories to be more like new games than reskins of the Haruspex - this is really admirable. I suppose none of this is really an "issue" and I wish them luck.

Anyway, £29.50 is a bit steep, but I'd say even for like £15 it is amazing. I got it for less than £5, and saw it just go up for even less. I feel like I've scammed the developers, it really is amazing.

"Pathologic 2" is a haunting and introspective masterpiece that defies traditional gaming conventions to deliver a deeply emotional and thought-provoking experience. Developed by Ice-Pick Lodge, this game is not just a narrative-driven adventure; it's a profound exploration of human nature, suffering, and the choices we make in dire circumstances.

At its core, "Pathologic 2" plunges players into a decaying town plagued by a mysterious and deadly disease. As the player assumes the role of one of three healers with unique perspectives, they navigate a web of interconnected stories, moral dilemmas, and existential crises amidst the town's impending demise.

The game's narrative is a labyrinth of emotions, ambiguity, and philosophical musings. Each character's journey intertwines with the lives of the townsfolk, revealing layers of despair, hope, desperation, and resilience. The writing is masterful, delving into themes of sacrifice, redemption, human frailty, and the fragility of life itself.

What sets "Pathologic 2" apart is its unflinching portrayal of suffering and the human condition. The game challenges players to confront difficult choices with no clear right or wrong answers, forcing them to grapple with ethical dilemmas, personal beliefs, and the consequences of their actions on others. The sense of moral weight and emotional depth permeates every decision, conversation, and interaction, creating a palpable atmosphere of tension and introspection.

The game's survival mechanics add layers of complexity and realism to the experience. Players must manage resources, maintain their character's health, hunger, and exhaustion, and navigate a harsh and unforgiving world. This adds a sense of urgency and immersion, mirroring the struggles of the townsfolk as they fight for survival amidst chaos and despair.

Visually, "Pathologic 2" is a hauntingly beautiful game, with a stark art style that captures the bleakness and decay of the town. The atmospheric sound design, haunting music, and environmental details enhance the sense of immersion, drawing players deeper into the game's haunting narrative and emotional landscape.

The game's pacing is deliberate and methodical, allowing moments of quiet introspection amidst the chaos and urgency of the unfolding events. This pacing invites players to reflect on their choices, relationships, and the broader themes of the game, creating a profound and personal connection to the narrative and characters.

In conclusion, "Pathologic 2" is a rare gem in gaming—a deeply emotional and intellectually stimulating experience that transcends the medium's boundaries. It challenges players to confront uncomfortable truths, wrestle with moral ambiguity, and explore the depths of human emotion and resilience in the face of adversity. For those seeking a profound and unforgettable journey into the human psyche, "Pathologic 2" is an absolute must-play.

I didn’t really play Pathologic 2 myself. I bought it, poked around in the opening chapters, and then bailed to a playthrough because the game seriously gave me the heebie-jeebies. Still, I went in expecting a straightforward psychological horror thriller, and what I found instead was one of the most powerful portrayals of what it feels like to try reconnecting with your heritage after having abandoned it to assimilate into modern society.

The game tells of a town on the edge of the steppe where a sickness takes hold and reason falters. Its people cling to rites and old faiths, they barter and gossip. The plague moves, and it moves fast. There is no hero’s work to be done here - only the long endurance of some puppet who knows, or should know at least, that survival is hard and the road is long. Time passes more quickly with each remaining day.

You play a surgeon returned from exile, a man bound by debt and bound by blood. Your hands can heal but never enough. Every decision costs something dear. To help one soul is to abandon another. Food runs out. Sleep is rare and shallow. Even the smallest kindness bears a shadow. Overall, the game’s stat systems (thirst, hunger, stamina...) are cruel but fair, as nature is 'fair'.

They do not mock you.
They only ask that you understand.

The writing is plain and deliberate, carrying a sort of mythic sorrow. Existential grief, you could call it. There are no revelations, only recognitions. Many a conversation reveals and thus, reopens wounds. Yet there is life in the town, in its superstition and in its hunger, and in the faces of those who still expect mercy. You come to know them, and when they die you carry their absence like a stone in your pocket. And as it gets heavier, you take every chance you can get to forget about your own burden, your own heavy heart, still beating in spite of everything.

What the game achieves is not pleasure but gravity. It reminds you that survival is a moral act, that knowledge cannot save anyone, and that faith is a thing both poisoned and necessary.

When it ends, there is no triumph, only the stillness of a place that outlasts its inhabitants. You put it down changed, and not entirely for the better.

Recommendation? Sure. If you call yourself a gamer and all you do is play Call Of Duty etc, this game isn't probably for you. Yeah, it's one of those rare games where I am still processing what happened to my character/the game world and I need to compress it internally before I can restart a new game. And while doing so, I need to play something else. I'm not ready to return.

All in all, Pathologic 2 is full of jank, the ugly washed up textures, weird design choices (ie. have some spoken dialogue but it's 99% text) but with the abnormal writing style and continuous rule bending, it still manages to rise towards a 9/10 game. Not perfect in any means but very unique.

2. Open Boot.Config and change gfx-enable-gfx-jobs from 0 to 1

3. Add gfx-enable-native-gfx-jobs=1 underneath the above line 

4. Go to C:\Users\Your User Name\AppData\LocalLow\Ice-Pick Lodge\Pathologic 2\Settings

Pathologic 2 is not a game that you play. It is a game that you go to war with. Unfortunately, your army is equipped with sticks and slings, whilst the enemy forces have fully automatic weapons and state of the art drones. In spite of this however, you are asked, not only to persevere, but succeed. This game was made by sadists who enjoy watching other people suffer - and it is glorious. 

Pathologic 2 is an oppressively difficult game, so much so that the developers actually had to add difficulty options post-launch due to public outcry, much to their own dissatisfaction as I understand it. If you play on the intended difficulty (and you should) you will find a game that kicks you while you are down and spits on your face. It is unforgiving and it relishes in that fact. When you die in this game, you are punished for it, you'll lose max health and max hunger bar which is very rough for a survival game. However, the difficulty of this game adds so much to the atmosphere that it makes the tension of the game almost palpable. There are other games out there that have world ending plots that aren't even a quarter as tense as this game is. This game will take you on a roller coaster of emotions. Most of those emotions will be stress-adjacent, but the ones that aren't are so powerful. This game offers a sense of earned-catharsis that rival and even surpass the Fromsoft games.

Dying in this game is very unforgiving and you SHOULD be afraid of death. However, you should be more afraid of giving up. This game has so much to offer and death is just part of the experience. You play as one of the few doctors in an eastern European town that is being relentlessly assaulted by plague, famine, crime and all manner of otherworldly things and it is your job to keep it together. Sound stressful? You don't know the half of it, because while you are doing that you also need to make sure to eat, sleep, drink, check up on people in town and be a doctor. In doing these duties, you will become engrossed in a unique world that is so different to anything that the current video game market has to offer. With excellent dialogue, endearing characters, solid survival game play and a fantastic atmosphere to tie it all together, I could not recommend this game more if I tried. If you're interested in a single-player, story driven, survival game with real consequences, play Pathologic 2.

A modern masterpiece, one that is sadly overlooked. My usual format for Pathologic 2 doesn't quite work here, because it's a game unlike anything I've ever played before, apart from my brief go at the original Pathologic of course.

Pathologic 2 is essentially a remake of 1. But even then calling it a simple remake is doing a disservice to both games, as it earns the 2 in its title due to some clever narrative motifs. It's a do-over, a take two of the first game on many interesting levels, thus you won't need to play Pathologic 1 to enjoy 2.

On the surface, Pathologic 2 is a survival game with elements of horror built on top of immersive sim design; it's a game that makes you uneasy, dreading the challenges you're about to face, fearing for the fates of the characters you love and constantly pressuring you to look after yourself as you survive a truly terrible plague. How you go about surviving the harsh town on the Gorkhon or whether you should use your medical skills to find a cure for such a terrible foe that beset the people is entirely up to you, freedom of choice but almost every choice you make has great consequences.

Everything is a resource; your health, your needs, your reputation, your crafting items, your weapons, your common folk and even your time is all a resource, a currency even. You're always having to trade something off to do something else, you will never be able to do everything so you need to manage everything wisely, plan well ahead of time and choose who should live even if it means someone else has to die. 

The story, world building, characters, etc are all absolutely phenomenal - the writing alone in the story was more than enough to keep me hooked on what's going on and that writing is so good, so well thought out, so meaningful that almost everything everyone says has some hidden meaning. Small inconsequential details almost always culminate into some major revelation, giving you an insight in what characters think even if they don't say it out loud - the game kept me constantly reading between the lines and even then it still managed to surprise me where every big story moment hit as hard as it should have.

The game's systems allows for some great emergent storytelling with the characters who can die, some huge arcs can be completely missed if you neglect others, and seemingly normal conversations can hit so much harder when the plague takes those who you live the most, allowing for some really emotional and impactful moments that other games simply don't have. The game's treatment of important characters dying in the most uneventful way possible, treating them as just another statistic of dead townsfolk, just twists the knife in your heart ever deeper.

Sure there are some issues; performance leaves a lot to be desired, some animations are straight up not very good to say the least and it is technically an unfinished game. But elements other people see as flaws such as the janky combat, the punishing difficulty and such are totally intentional - because you are Artemy Burakh; a healer, not a fighter. Your job to keep the sick treated, to find out how to beat the plague and to save as many lives as possible. The game even makes a remark multiple times to not get into fights and to take good care of yourself as much as possible, combat should only be an absolute last resort option to keep yourself alive or if you manage to get the jump on your enemies via stealth or stocked up on powerful firearms to get much needed supplies. But even then you will spend resources, you will have to repair those weapons, bandage up your wounds, etc, and all of that can cost precious other resources, reputation and, most importantly, time.

Is it an unfair game? Yes, absolutely. But don't let that dissuade you from playing Pathologic 2, because that struggle is built into the core systems and even the storytelling, and most importantly the presentation of that storytelling. It takes some incredibly clever, weird and meta turns in how it presents its narrative and "the point" of what Pathologic 2 is trying to convey to the audience - which is you, the player. And like I said, the story alone is absolutely worth the trials and tribulations ahead because the pay offs of those arduous build-ups is always worth it, every single time.

Honestly, I can gush all day about this amazing game, if you have a friend who talks your ear off about Pathologic 2, then just know there's a VERY good reason why they do, because I honestly can't recommend it enough. It really is that incredible, so much so it's easily in my top 10 games of all time, I'm already excited to do a replay to see how differently things can play out if I approach everything in different ways. 

Even at full price I strongly recommend you play Pathologic 2, there's a ton of game to sink your teeth into with about 25-35 hours for a first playthrough and it is filled to the brim with incentives to replay. And if you find it too tough then don't despair, because the game allows you to tweak as many elements as you could possibly with some of the best difficulty customisation I've ever seen in a game, you can't get rid of that challenge entirely but it is approachable to many people. And can also be made so much more dread-inducing to veterans of the game, if you're a glutton for punishment.

Pathologic 2 is a challenging game, but the difficulty is done in such a way that it adds to the experience rather than detracting from it.

The resource scarcity forces tough decisions, items you need to survive are also needed to save NPCs from the plague. Combat is high-risk, and dying comes with penalties that persist across saves. Every choice can cost vital resources, which are often better spent elsewhere.

Time is probably the most valuable resource. You won’t be able to do everything or save everyone. You have to prioritize which objectives to complete, often at the expense of others. Do you take the shortcut through plague-stricken districts at great risk to yourself, or take the long way around and spare your immunity boosters?

The game is bizarre, harsh, and utterly compelling. "Fun" isn't quite the word I’d use to describe it, the game seems to work against you at every turn, but overcoming its challenges is deeply satisfying, and it makes for a really memorable playthrough.

I thought a lot how to really put it. A work of art, an animated drama novel, survival game as it supposed to be, and so on. All of it just won't do. Then I recalled a conversation with a friend, which we had in times of struggles. And so I found my own words to describe it.
"Life is never fair. What are you going to do about it?"

The game itself, as an actual game, is not the masterpiece of technology, even slightly flawed visually and mechanically, but in a way that does not breaks the impression, and with amount of meticulously thought through, immersive details, you may not even notice most of technical jankiness. Despite technical perfection never being game's main strength, it still uses all it could for building of very impressive, immersive atmosphere.

The story is.. wild, to say the least. Despite seemingly simple premise, it is full of human characters, interactions, motivation, and events, outright worthy of Dostoevsky novel. The game openly invites you to participate in intrigues, opinions, grudges and motivations of characters who actually resemble humans, with their own stories and angles.

Survival is hard. Really hard. As many reviewers already mentioned, it is hard up to the point of being unfair. It is so, but there's a thing - it is hard not because of technical difficulties, or because the game outright cheats you. It is hard because the game directly says to you - it is all about your own decisions, take it or leave it. There will be no hand-holding, there will be no justice, there will be no happy ending. Life is never fair, and you are just one pawn among many in fate's hands. What are you going to do about it?

In fact, the game says so to properly condition you - there will be hints, but you have to be aware to spot them. There will be help, but it will cost you dearly. There will be decisions which you see as definitely right ones, which will lead to disasters just because you are so used to narrow vision, used to fairytales of heroism, so you can't often see the full picture. The game pulls the rug under you feet constantly not because it is strictly unfair, but to genuinely challenge you - life is never fair. Your decision could be in fact not yours, just someone's whisper in your mind which you heard. Unfolding events could be not in your control, since you are never the center of human world, just a part of it. Your own prosperity could be not something granted due to "rights and privileges", but something you have to fight for. All you have in your life - your own judgement, and your actions, which you throw at fate and see if you can wipe this wicked grin from Death's face. What are you going to do about it? You are nothing but an actor on life's stage, and all you can do - is to play your role as you see fit.

The game will mock you openly, taunt you, suggest you to put it away, to play something easier, where after each learned hop and trick some master would reward with tiny piece of mental sugar. Don't listen to it, carry on, and think - if you're an actor in grand theatre of Life and Death, it does not matters how badly you perform, as long as you perform genuinely, tapping into your own emotions and creativity, finding your own ways in the face of unbearable or even impossible odds. It is a game about you.

Wherever you are, dear player, and whatever moment of life you're in, never give up on life, even when struggling with something seemingly impossible to defeat. Only after delving deep into pits of desperation and hopelessness, you may truly learn how to appreciate little moments of your life, appreciate people around you, and the fact that life's play is not about achievements. It is about your own story.

Life is never fair. But it is always about what you are going to do with it.

[h1] Battling the Abyss: A Deep Dive into Pathologic 2 [/h1]

Alright, let's dive into the rabbit hole that is Pathologic 2. Trust me, it's not your everyday gaming experience. It's more like a plunge into a surreal, feverish dream where survival is a tightrope walk and decisions are as heavy as they come.

Imagine a town strangled by a lethal plague, and you, a native, are handed the Herculean task of curbing it in just 12 days. Pathologic 2 isn't just about survival; it's about sacrifice. Every move, every choice has a cost, some big enough to keep you up at night. The plague is ruthless, time is ticking, and the town's eerie atmosphere is suffocating.

The game unfolds like a tragic play. You're Artemy Burakh, fighting not just the pandemic but also the enigmatic steppe culture and your own demons. The survival struggle is real, my friend. Resources deplete faster than hope, and every day is a gauntlet of trial and error. Survival isn't a given; it's earned through grit and resource juggling.

Now, let's talk about the game's uniqueness. Pathologic 2 doesn't pull punches. It doesn't just show a bleak world; it thrusts you into it. Failure isn't an option; it's a reality that echoes for hours. The game weaves its mechanics into the atmosphere seamlessly. This isn't Fallout, where survival is a choice; it's a demand, an unyielding force shaping your every move.

Pathologic 2 is not everyone's cup of tea, and that's okay. Its survival mechanics might be too intense for some, its dramatic dialogue too flowery for others. But here's the thing—games like this, unapologetically bold, are what makes this medium extraordinary. It's a masterpiece, a revisiting of a captivating concept that stumbled before (Pathologic Classic). This is art that doesn't just flirt with the term 'game'; it dances with it.

I've made mistakes, damned friends, and glimpsed into the abyss. Pathologic 2 is an experience that doesn't just linger; it haunts. It's a journey where contradictions flourish, and surviving is an art in itself. The game's eerie atmosphere and surrealism keep you in the dark, and the details that stick are the most unsettling.

Now, the nitty-gritty. The survival game mechanics, while daunting, are the backbone. The plague hits hard, and as Artemy, you're a part of the ruthless race against time. Autopsies, trading antibiotics for jerky, embracing folk traditions—it's a wild ride, and every choice bites back.

Yes, it's frustrating. Starving, collapsing, racing against time—it mirrors the bleak narrative. Every decision's a gamble, a compromise between Artemy's well-being and others' survival. In this game, there are no winners, only survivors.

And if you think death's a way out, think again. Artemy dies, sure, but it's not the end. It's a twisted encore. The game gets harder; survival gets trickier. Death's a detour, not a dead end.

Pathologic 2 is a surreal drama draped in the tattered clothes of a survival game. It's not fun in the conventional sense, but it's brilliant. The plague, twisted dialogue, and ruthless mechanics blend into a haunting symphony. It won't be everyone's cup of tea, but it's a masterpiece in its own right.

This is one of the best games that - in good conscious - I cannot recommend to anyone other than true masochists. Pathologic 2 is definitely not for everyone. However...To anyone who is looking for a memorable experience, can accept the game for what is it, and commit to sticking with it, you won't be disappointed. Even when frustrated and dying, I still loved this game.

At its heart, Pathologic 2 is a brutal survival game wrapped in a horror blanket. The atmosphere is top notch as the game does a beautiful job at making you feel like you a part of this bleak, breathing (yet dying) world. Time passes regardless of what you are doing meaning events will play out even if you're not there. The fact that entire quest lines can be missed or have dire consequences because you were focused on something or someone else can feel overwhelming; but it is also one of the intriguing factors of the game. It (along with multiple endings) also gives you a reason to go through the game again so you can learn more about the world and its lore while helping NPCs you may have shunned or overlooked the first time. 

With that said, this is also where some of Pathologic 2's charm becomes its shortcoming. As I said earlier, it is a survival game and time passes regardless of what you're doing. You have multiple stats to keep a close eye on: health, infection, exhaustion, hunger, and thirst/stamina. On the surface, these should be relatively easy stats to manage. Hungry? Just eat food. Tired? Just sleep a bit. However, resources are very limited with over world item spawns being random, and precious time is still marching on. This means that you are going to find yourself in multiple situations where you have to pick between doing a quest or rummaging through trash cans and cabinets to find anything to prevent yourself from dying. Or risk missing something important to take a quick nap so you don't die of exhaustion.

Another aspect of Pathologic 2 - which is both its strength and weakness - is the fact that the game is cryptic and won't really tell you how to do anything. Do you know how bartering works? Do you know how to brew tinctures? Do you know what items are super rare and hard to get? No? Well go figure it out. Pathologic 2 greatly encourages you to learn through trial and error which is something I love but also can be frustrating. If you play on the intended difficulty, Pathologic 2 is very unforgiving and punishes you for mistakes by permanently decreasing your stat bars. Granted, you can absolutely beat the game without max stats because let's be real, you're never going to be truly full, healthy, and well rested in this world (just like real life). Yet, it still can be demoralizing, especially when your death was caused by something you had no idea how to avoid or could even happen. 

Yet, there is a great sense of accomplishment by finally figuring out how to live in this world even if it means restarting a couple days or your whole playthrough depending on how far you are. It's very satisfying when you do get yourself in a decent position where you're rested enough and stocked with a bit of food to where you can focus more on the story vs. searching desperately for resources. It is challenging to get to that point, and I can understand why (according to Steam achievements), nearly 3/4 of players stopped at Day 3. But it's all worth it for the incredible story that you piece together overtime.

For those who want something challenging, satisfying, creepy, mysterious, and encourages you to come back for more... Pathologic 2 is the 100% game for you!

[h1]It may sound basic but it's when things go wrong that Pathologic shines[/h1]

Without going into spoilers, depending on certain factors like the day, decisions made, people neglected, etc.
The townsfolk get put in danger, all those people you get introduced to can and probably will die without intervention.
The hard part is managing your resources, like weapons, food, medicine and most assuredly... Time!

With each passing day, times grows shorter and shorter, at first you may not notice it but as the days go on, you'll find that the game ain't lying. Your hunger depletes more rapidly, you find longer events may not be worth the time investment, and each day brings new problems that helped me understand the general gameplay systems by force.

Things only get worse as you'll need resources to make it through the day, and as the days go on, things get worse.
Stockpiling is a massive boon but can be hard in practice, looting houses is a mixed bag of results for a variety of reasons but bartering can get you far.
Trading for items and figuring out what people want can be the difference between life and death, make use of it.

[h1]Life is unfair, and that's (mostly) alright[/h1]

Despite the survival gameplay being harsh and time being hard to manage (you can't be everywhere and do everything), things can be relatively managable, but sometimes the game will decide to mess with you.
Sometimes people are put in danger or straight up killed based on chance, while there's stuff you can do to mitigate that, odds are you'll run out of luck eventually and have to live with it [spoiler]or savescum but please don't[/spoiler].
 
While certain interactions will change, you're never really outright punished for a characters death, life goes on and you will make it to the end so long as you persevere, but there is one lasting consequence you might end up cursing, and that's your own death.
Outside of day 1, the town remembers how many times you've died, regardless of reloading, and will punish you as it sees fit.
From lowered max health to worse loot, it can only make your life harder, but it's NOT the end of things.
The punishments start out tame and like I said, the town remembers, while it's mostly the punishments that will remind you of your death, there are other reminders that are decently interesting to encounter.

[h1]Speaking of the town[/h1]

An incredibly odd mix of rustic environments colliding with almost cult-esque themes.
Most of the houses look normal, if a bit copy/paste, but then you'll spot structures that defy the laws of gravity, massive towers meant to house the work population and the scenic steppe belonging to the local tribe with it's "odd" people that isn't even taking into account their culture and exploitation.

This is the thing that ultimately got my attention, and while you'll see a lot of what it has to offer pretty quickly, there's still info waiting to be uncovered which makes it interesting.

[h1]But there are some downright bad comments to make[/h1]

Combat is quite frankly just bad, it's incredibly easy to stunlock most enemies to the point where I would say my preferred weapon was my bare fists, but realistically it was my legs as running away is mad easy. Considering how combat is frowned upon by the local population and knives/guns can drain my health from full to nothing in a second, I'd much rather just leave it alone whenever possible.

While I think the death system is very cool, there's little reason not to reload before you think something goes wrong as, when you die, it just boots you back to your previous save anyway, so you might just be in a very similar spot that lead to your death without any escape other loading even further back.

While I did want to keep the town population alive, I'd be lying if I said I cared for even half this cast, as most times I try and interact with them they just don't have any dialogue, usually needing an event to trigger conversation, this makes wandering around the town feel downright pointless at times, especially as certain places become empty as people start dying.

Thirst feels kind of pointless, it's rather easy to maintain and to my understanding, never decreases past a certain threshold, making it the only meter you don't actually have to manage for survival outside of stockpiling your sprint duration.

[h1]If you're interested, go into it with the expectation that this is something different and will use its difficulty to try and sell a setting instead of appealing to a larger demographic[/h1]

It's hard, but fair, and personally I thought the experience was well worth it.
It might be boring, stressful or annoying at times but it works FAR more often than it doesn't.
If you're looking for something different, would highly recommend.

I am writing this review upon my third playthrough of this game - I can't believe I put myself through the torture of the console version twice before playing it on PC. The PC version is a massive improvement from console in regards to optimization, graphics, and bugs. If you've been hesitant to buy the PC version after playing on console - don't be. It is absolutely worth it to experience this masterpiece as intended.

This is one of the most unique experiences gaming has to offer. Similar to that of Russian literature, this story involves one of the most tragically beautiful blend of spiritual themes and philosophies I've seen in a video game. The developers use of Eurasian folklore brings attention to a topic that I feel isn't widely discussed, and I really appreciate that. 

Pathologic 2 is an anti-power fantasy where the main character... really isn't even the main character once you dig in and peel back the layers. Your choices in this game can reveal a lot about yourself while drawing lines between surgeon Artemy's history and the secrets of his small Steppe hometown of Gorkhon. While the RPG elements are fairly linear regarding dialogue, this game emphasizes that you can't do everything and you can't save everyone, offering you only your free will to complete the tasks that are important to you with time as your only limitation. A fascinating thing about this game's mechanics is that time will always move forward. No matter what you're doing, whether you're working the hospital, talking to townsfolk, playing hide and seek with the local orphans or sleeping, things will happen and the opportunity to interact with these things will pass - much like in real life. When you aren't engaged in conversation you will run around frantically at times scavenging to collect supplies, running from person to person to perform your doctoral duties while also maintaining your own health needs, running from thugs... or towards them if you prefer to fight head on, crafting folk medicine, and managing your sparse inventory space.

The design of this game is one of my favorite aspects, especially regarding environment. A big difference I have noticed between experiencing this on console and PC is how detailed the weather can be and how that can change the mood of the day in game. As you move deeper into the pandemic, the weather has a tendency to get foggier, rainier, and darker, whereas at the beginning of the game you bask in much more sunlight. The architectural elements of this game is also interesting, and plays a huge role in explaining the town's history. As a survival horror/dark fantasy game, you will find some of the most intimidating parts of the map to actually end up being the safest, forcing you to accept and even seek comfort in the dark.

Knowing how few people complete this game based on achievement history across platforms with a massive drop off after the plague hits, I'd like to add this to the discussion: I'm not going to pretend this game is easy in gameplay or easy to get through with it's heavy themes. It's not. It's quite frustrating at times and incredibly challenging and honestly sometimes really uncomfortable to sit through. If you're reading this and have avoided playing this game because of the potential for frustration - don't!! Experiencing this game is so rewarding and failure is part of the experience (and even leads to unlocking new bits of lore at times!!) 

All in all, this is one of my favorite games of all time and I wish I could see this series get more traction. Thank you, devs, for this work of art.

Pathologic 2 is a truly incredible and unique experience. It's not for everyone, in fact I would go so far as to say it's not for most people. But if you're intrigued enough to read reviews, it may just be for you. Everything I'm about to say applies to the game's intended and hardest difficulty, which I recommend you play on.
 Here's why this game is genius: the goal of most games is to be fun and satisfying for the player. All their systems are tailored to achieve that. The goal of this game is to produce a state of stress, anxiety, and desperation in the player -*but also a sense of hope, a sense that you can win.* All its systems are finely tuned to enable you to stay on top of the various things dragging you down (hunger, lack of time, exhaustion) - but only by the skin of your teeth. As you come to understand it more, you realize that the game, despite going to great lengths to seem unfair, is in fact very fair - it always gives you access to the things you need to survive and win, as long as you pay attention and plan carefully. But your life in the game is never easy, you always have tough choices to make, and relief is only ever temporary. This combination is what makes it so engaging - not to speak about the story, world and characters, which are all wonderfully weird and vivid. 
Only about 7% of players have the achievement for beating the game on its intended difficulty. Clearly, these design principles don't click for everybody. But if or when they do, this game becomes the most mesmerizing and compelling game out there.

You play as a doctor in a town that gets ravaged by a plague and the entire gameplay loop is essentially trying to balance saving people around you, doing objectives (some of which might save people's lives or work towards solving problems), all while making sure you don't get sick or die of hunger/sleep deprivation. You can't do everything, so time management is basically the entire game. It makes you feel pretty awful and I was stressed for what feels like 95% of my play time. That being said, I enjoyed it and will likely give it another go when I have the time. I appreciate how it doesn't pull any punches, it never says "oh well he was doing a big objective that took all day, we'll give him a pass and not let this character die." No, you wasted your day, or you chose your priorities, you live with the consequences. Not many games are willing to do that and potentially piss off the player to such a harsh extent. 

I also appreciate how unclear everything is. A lesser game would just say outright "work on the cure today or go out and help people?" Instead, you get a cluster fuck of "What objectives should I go after? How can I make a cure in a town in the middle of nowhere with so little technology? Will this objective even help me find a cure or is it a waste of time? Will it be beneficial in other ways? This character says there's something important I need to see way outside of town which will take time to get to, do I go to him or do I spend that time making and distributing immunity boosters?" etc. It's an absolutely crazy, unforgiving, horrible mess in the best way.

If any of this sounds interesting to you then give it a go, just make sure you get past the weird prologue (really turned me off tbh) and into the actual game itself. Once you're there you'll know if it's something you'll like or absolutely hate.

Pathologic begins at its end. You find yourself there, a failure, begging for another shot. [i] We just didn’t have enough time [/i] . It is not until you fail your first playthrough that this opening scene, or closing scene, really starts to make sense. What’s with the white masks, and the birds, and why has the theater been repurposed to a hospital? Step outside and find yourself walking through more than just foreshadowing; this is the end! Or is it? Can your actions change your fate? 

	Let me start with the criticisms. Pathologic is an unforgiving game. If you cannot embrace failure and tribulation it may not be your cup of twyrine. It is a beautiful game in many regards, but the animations leave much to be desired. There is not full voice acting, so get ready to read—a lot. When was the last time you read a good book? For those who played the first game, it may be disappointing to hear that of the three playable characters in the first one, each with a unique experience, only one is available in this game, and that is unlikely to change due to this games lukewarm commercial success. That being said, it is a fantastic game regardless, and gave me about 30 hours of content on my first playthrough. 

	If you are still reading, maybe you have not been turned away yet. This game has a lot to stay for, so let’s start with its story. The dialogue in this game can be a bit cryptic, but think of the dialogue as this game’s primary mechanic. Like any difficult game, it takes time to learn, but once you do it makes more sense. Characters can be unreliable and deceitful, and they will hold information from you. They speak in riddles, and metaphors, but it's not simply a bad translation or meaningless drivel. Some things may not make sense, even until a second playthrough, but they are important, and you must read everything if you want to have a clue what is going on. And, unlike the average AAA RPG, dialogue choices can carry enormous consequences, and even completely change the trajectory of the game. The narrative itself has elements of magic realism, mystery, horror, and theater. It synthesizes these genres well, into what is a very unique gaming experience. Overall, I really love it, but others may find its enigmatic style a bit grating. 

	Moving on, this game has a great visual art direction. This redeems any shortcomings in animations or mechanics for me. It is simply stunning. It combines the styles of gothic, macabre, and surreal art with a good dose of Russian industrialism. These are juxtaposed against what is likely the Siberian Steppe in a speculative past, along with a great soundtrack, to create something as unsettling as it is beautiful. 

	Finally, the gameplay itself. This is a mixed bag. I would not be writing this if I did not enjoy parts of it, but I do have some frustrations as well. There is a lot of walking in this game, and it can get kind of old. There are ferries that act as fast travel points, but the currency used to travel is sparse. The combat is exceptionally janky, but serviceable, and luckily can usually be avoided. But if you are looking for a game where combat and action are the main attraction, look elsewhere. 

	For me, Pathologic is one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve had. If you give this game a chance, I do not think you will be disappointed. This is a truly unique experience that pushes the boundaries of its medium. Whatever you do, don't listen to Aspity. Talk to [i] her [/i] first.

[h3] Pathologic 2: A Game That Breaks You And Remakes You [/h3]

Some games are difficult. Some games are punishing. Pathologic 2 is something else entirely. It doesn’t just test your skills—it tests your limits, your values, your very sense of self.

From the moment you arrive in the plagued town, you realize this isn’t a story about winning. It’s about enduring. The air is thick with rot, the sky is heavy, as if mourning. The town itself seems to breathe in pain, its streets lined with fading footprints of those who won’t see another sunrise. 

[b] You are not a hero. You are not here to save everyone. You are here to survive—and survival is cruel.  [/b]

The game gives you just enough to scrape by, but never enough to feel safe. You will starve. You will grow weak. You will look into the eyes of the dying and know that you cannot help them. And the worst part? You will get used to it. It forces you to choose—who do you help? Who do you abandon? How much of your own humanity are you willing to sacrifice just to see another day?

At first, I fought against the system. I tried to play perfectly, to plan, to strategize. But Pathologic 2 doesn’t let you be perfect. It watches as you stumble, as you break, as your convictions crumble under the weight of starvation and despair. It strips away that illusion, forcing you to accept failure as an inevitability. It made me confront my own stubbornness, my own selfish need to "get it right." And when I finally let go of that, when I accepted that suffering and compromise were my only paths forward, the game transformed into something else entirely.

The town is alive—not just in its decaying streets and whispering corners, but in the weight of every choice you make. The faces you pass today may be corpses tomorrow. The laughter of children is a rare sound, swallowed by the hush of grief. The hunger gnaws at you like a rabid dog, and the exhaustion drapes over your body like a funeral shroud. Every meal you steal could be someone else’s last. Every step forward feels like trudging through the ashes of a world that no longer wants you in it.

[b] The world doesn’t revolve around you, and it never did. [/b]


Playing Pathologic 2 feels like drowning, yet somehow, you keep pushing forward. And when it finally lets you breathe, you realize you’ve come out the other side—changed, but never whole.

I can’t say this game is for everyone. But if you’re willing to suffer, to embrace the unknown, and to truly feel, it’s an experience unlike any other.

So Pathologic 2 is a remake/reimagining of the original Pathologic from 2005. The original allowed you to play 3 different characters to experience the game 3 different ways. Pathologic 2 however focuses only on the Haruspex character, a surgeon (emshen) named Artemy Burakh who has returned to his small isolated village at his father's behest only to find his father murdered and himself the prime suspect on Day 1. Queue the townspeople instantly hating you and beating the shit out of you on sight for 2 straight days as you attempt to get it all straightened out and find your father's murderer.

[b]AND THEN BAM. A PLAGUE.[/b]

Now you, the hated son-returned-home, are the man the town is (nearly) solely relying on to find a way to cure this ailment before everybody dies, as, for lore reasons, Artemy is the only man allowed to autopsy bodies. But you also gotta sprinkle in being the town's therapist, detective, chemist, marathon runner, Kin defender, father <3, and murderer or saint depending on your playstyle (look, Artemy’s going through a lot okay).

Now you have 12 days to figure it all out and keep your loved ones from dying.

And when the game says you can’t save everyone, it really really means it. From the start the game is punishing and as the days progress it only gets harder and harder. The fighting is quite wonky in this game, and your resources are very limited. Also everyone is fighting in the streets? Very dramatic stuff. Some of your most beloved characters are most definitely going to die, some quests each day are going to go unfinished, and sometimes the game might piss you off, but it’s worth pushing through despite it all. Many of the characters are quite lovable despite how strange they all act, and you’re gonna wanna keep them safe. Also the kids were my favorites despite the fact that they all talk like omnipotent beings lol. 

Now, the worldbuilding for this game is pretty insane. I thought it was gonna take place in some backwoods Russian town but instead we’re gifted a richly imaginative world with a lot of depth and lore. And despite said town being a microcosm of a larger world that we don’t see at all, we still somehow learn all about the different customs and rituals and beliefs of the Town and Steppe. It was all so rich and detailed and unique as hell (comparable to Disco Elysium imo).
Also, despite it’s longer length, it feels like the type of game that is begging to be played again. The next time I do I’ll play it at intended difficulty (and suffer). 

Anyway, it’s a very thought provoking and original piece of art, and even though there was only one playable character this time around, it didn’t feel like anything was missing. I’m so excited for the sequel and am excited to play as the loml, the pretentious Daniil (and then hopefully Changeling next).

At the end of the day I at least saved my kids and that's what mattered.

[h3]Introduction[/h3]
Pathologic 2 is an open-world horror RPG with emphasis on survival and it's story. From paper, the game seems fun and after completing it, I can assure you that it is really fun but I would wager that it is not everyone's cup of tea. If you're looking for action packed survival horror game, then this isn't for you. This is actually my first Pathologic game that I have played, I didn't play the first game before and I was really impressed by it.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
To start off, the gameplay might seem relatively easy from the surface, but every resources and choices you make counts towards your progression. The livelihood of the entire town is in your hand. You play as Arthemy Burakh or Haruspex, whichever you prefer and the story starts as you journey towards a remote town following your father's request. But upon arrival you found that he has been murdered. It might seem really overwhelm at first as not only there's the threat of plague looming around but you will need to find your father's murderer as well but the game list out your objective in a clear and precise manner that you can keep track of it easily. The game starts of relatively slow for the first 2 days I reckon but it gets better. Every choices you make counts and I really like this aspect of the game. Some characters might actually die due to your decisions and if you're not careful enough with your resources, you might actually die as well. The game challenges its player to manage their resources more carefully. You might get thirsty/hungry/exhausted much easier and will actually hinder your progress of the game. 

The game have a relatively large map and there is also fast travel available but there's a catch. You need "Fingernails" to be able to use the fast travel. This not only ensure that you will spend them wisely but it also encourages player to explore the open-world and interact with the characters around the map. Yes there is a downside to it, It might get tedious after awhile as most of the quest are conversation based and time is limited so it would be wise to use them carefully. There is combat mechanic however I tend to avoid them as it is really clunky. There are weapons and guns for you to choose from and here's something i think deserve a praise for. If the condition of your gun is low, the likelihood of it getting jam is higher. This realism really adds to the gameplay as it doesn't encourage the player to blindly rely on their weapons instead of figuring out other methods to take down the enemy. Have I mentioned that you need to purchase the gun?. The game really doesn't babysit apart from its tutorial during the earlier days and I like it. How you trade with other player, how you manage your food/water consumption and all the way to how you behave in every areas of the town will have great affect on your gameplay experience. The game is definitely hard but it is worth exploring as the story-telling is one of the best that I have played.

 [h3]Graphics & Music[/h3]
Moving on to the music, I really can't express enough how much I love it. All the way from the main menu theme to the abattoir, I really can't get enough of it. Everything just blends together so well. Kudos to the composer behind the OST. The graphics however are decent and really gives of the vibe that you're in a dire situation which is the point of this game. The character facial expression are also great and the voice actor/actress also did a good job portraying the characters.

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]
In Conclusion, the game is worth to pickup if you're into games with amazing story. As for the horror aspect, it is more of a psychology horror than supernatural horror and the way they did it is really impressive. It doesn't really on cheap jump scares, instead it relies on its story, as the player go through the day more and more, the more exposition come to light. I personally really like it and I feel like this is a game worth a shot if you're into story based games.

Had a good time with this one. Pathologic 2 is definitely an incredibly unique game with the way it's setup. I think something worth mentioning is that this game isn't for everyone as it can be incredibly punishing. With that being said, if you want an experience that will challenge you it's a great buy. 
   
   The gameplay pretty much comes down to a battle of resource management and decision making with timed pressure. The story progresses in a way where the clock is always ticking and regardless of what you do, will eventually reach the end. With this in mind you really can't afford to do everything on the map so you'll need to choose carefully. This is all the while keeping a close eye on your hunger, thirst and immunity meters as you navigate the plague running rampant. There were definitely a number of times where I struggled to keep things under control. Another interesting factor is that doing more isn't always better. You never know how certain interactions will influence the game state.
   
   I would say the most impressive thing about the game is the atmosphere. The soundtrack does a great job at keeping you on edge in the day to day. A lot of the character interactions can give the game a certain eerie vibe that really sold it further. The way the color palette and weather changes also contributes plenty. Overall I found myself highly immersed and liked this aspect of the game the most.
    
   If I were to make any criticisms it would be that hunger could stand to be just slightly more manageable (not too much, just a bit). It can be rather overwhelming to deal with sometimes so it might have been beneficial to tune the numbers to not be as intense while still not being easy. The other thing that comes to mind is performance. I have a high end GPU but still found the framerate to dip a lot with higher settings. With that being said, I don't think these things diminished my experience too much. It will be nice to see if Pathologic 3 can improve the technical foundation for more stable framerates.
     
   Overall I had a great experience with Pathologic 2 and will easy recommend it to anyone looking for a unique and also challenging experience. I don't think I've ever played something quite like it.

Graphics/sound quality 7/10: This game is not new by any means, and there is some parts of it that look janky/uncanny valley with the characters. There is a lot of weight to your decisions and actions in the game, but the pacing of movement as well as the clunky inputs can often be frustrating. This frustration can be compounding as you get further into the game and run into your own consequences. The only reason I give it a decent score is because that is partially intended. You’re returning to the place you grew up in only to find out it is not your home anymore. Instead, it rejects you like a foreign organ, forcing you into a life on the periphery, on the outside looking into a place where your birthright once was to belong. What happened? You realize the tethers to this life are worn and some have snapped already in your absence. Do you mend the broken strings or weave anew with threads you’ve once ignored? 
To me, Pathologic is about perseverance in the face of grief (or Grief, hehe), about continuing to fight despite everything and everyone you have lost already. It’s about bloodily carving a place for yourself in a community that rejects you, about the ways people love and the ways that love eats them up from the inside out. It’s about how sometimes life gives you no winning options and all you can do is Lose A Little Less Bad and in that, it forces you to reevaluate what it even means to lose. 
On my first playthrough, I restarted after I lost my first character. On my second playthrough, I lost them again. I was going to start over but I reached out to a friend who told me that I had to face it and get through it. Better luck next time. He was right. I found a way I could have saved them a few in-game days later. Had I not continued despite my (genuine!) sadness at their passing, I would’ve never gotten much further. 
I believe the reason the game wants you to fail (and you know it does, you’ve probably watched the hbomberguy video just the same as me) is not primarily to make you suffer along with your character. I think it’s about showing you that you can and will keep going despite it. This game doesn’t want your frustration, it wants your defiance. It wants you to look at all the hours you’ve already wasted walking through God’s Most Depressing Russian Town, all the health and items you’ve already lost, all the people you’ve already lost and go “I don’t care. Because there is something left for me here and that something, as little as it is, is worth fighting for”. 
Now here’s the thing about this humble reviewer specifically: I’m soft. I can’t kill people in video games because it makes me feel bad, I cry when people are mean to pigeons and were I not a little intellectually understimulated by games that don’t make me suffer a little you’d probably find me in the animal crossing review section ONLY. And I’m pretty sure that’s the only reason the game worked so well for me. You need to be willing to connect to this game on a visceral level, you need to be willing to feel for the fake people in your computer. I need you to play this one with your heart. Otherwise it’s just a weird game about being bad at hitting.

This game sucked me into it's world and made me connect with it and the characters in a way I never have before in other games. The more I learned about the world and the characters the more alive it all became. I started to care for these people as if they were my own friends and loved ones. In classic survival-horror fashion you will have to manage resources, explore and learn about the world, and uncover the mysteries of the town and it's inhabitants. This game is incredibly difficult; I spent most of the game on the brink of starvation and exhaustion but it only enriched the experience. It's not meant to be easy, you are meant to struggle along and push yourself to keep going against all odds.

I have another 50+ hours on GoG, I bought the game twice over because I love it so much and the developers have created a true work of art.
