The short answer: One is fortunate to recognize the tallest mountain they will ever climb as while descending from its summit - but I experienced just that as Pathologic 2's final page turned.

I've winded three (long) years down my own road since I turned P2's last page, but its echoes ring out undiminished - the curtain never quite finished falling.

The long answer:

Pathologic 2 is nothing less than the finest meditation on the human condition committed to a video game. Those of earnest heart, seeking to find their own humanity in a world whose only constant seems to be in-humanity and abject cruelty, will find Pathologic 2 indispensable.

This is a story for the orphans, the alienated and the cast away - the atheists/agnostics and the questioning theists doubting absentee gods in the sky. Pathologic has no interest in tall tales of [i]heavenly[/i] divinity or anthropomorphic Gods.

This is a story about [i]humanity's[/i] past and future: our realities, the stories we weave, our struggles, our hopes and dreams. You will find humans of all forms in the Town-On-Gorkhon; many are as you know, some like none you have ever seen, but no less human.

Speaking as clinically depressed person with deep-set embitterment and near universal misanthropy, this is one of few works to ever successfully penetrate that 10-mile deep neurological blockade in my mind and deliver a message of beauty.

To me Pathologic is:
[list]
    [*] Carl Sagan in his impassioned declaration in [i]The Pale Blue Dot[/i] that we must take our stand here and now - that neither gods nor visitors from above will intervene to save us;
    [*] David Foster Wallace, in his finest essays and elaborations on depression and mental health struggles;
    [*] Van Gogh in his heart-rending study of beauty and grief in works like [i]Sorrowing Man (At Eternity's Gate)[/i];
    [*] Scorcese's [i]Taxi Driver[/i] in its compassion for the troubled war vet drowning in a society that has abandoned him; the kinds of people we are so keen to write off;
    [*] The wistful contemplations and transcendent humanism of the lonely bard in Zeppelin's [i]Stairway to Heaven[/i];
    [*] The final reflections in the Jisei (death poems) of condemned Japanese men;
[/list],

It takes full advantage of its format to tell a story of synchronicity - disconnected threads converge, weaving a vivid web of tragedy and triumph.

It is impossible to talk about Pathologic without acknowledging its inexorably Slavic roots and worldview. We are a commonly overlooked ethnic group, and this game represents our absolute best - it's up there with my other favorite work of fiction [i]Пикник На Обочине AKA Roadside Picnic[/i], adapted into Tarkovsky's equally inimitable [i]Stalker[/i]. Like those, this is not a story of bombast and adventure, but quiet introspection.

I will take only a minimal aside to state that yes, Pathologic 2's [i]gameplay experience[/i] is absolutely enjoyable, intense, challenging and rewarding. However, to clumsily surgically deconstruct this work into its components would be a [i]tremendous insult[/i] to the "whole body" Ice-Pick Lodge have constructed here.

I would be remiss to not mention P2's most touching substory. P2 contains the most complex, endearing, remarkable characterizations of children and young people I have ever seen in any work. The protagonist and I started our journey with no affection for children, but through the most terrible of storms we found just that - a wholesome love for, [i]particularly[/i] a couple of scruffy orphans.

Offer them the patient kindness you wished adults had shown you in your youth; [b]do not[/b] miss a moment when your charges call on you; when the curtain falls for the last time, you'll find a bond forged-in-flame, lying on the stairs where you three [u]stand together[/u]. 

Pathologic 2 is a gothic, grim, challenging fable replete with all-too-human visions of horror and misery - but from the roiling inferno rises that great bird, belting out its stirring, optimistic, sincere call to our better angels - revealing love, staggering beauty, and redemption.

Pathologic 2 can be unfair to you quite frequently, but every death is a lesson on how better to navigate the enemies and the hunger and thirst mechanics.

This along with 1 are some of the most dread filled amazing games ive ever played. Everything feels so *off* and wrong but UNDERSTANDABLE about the methods this town and world creates.

You can't save everyone, and you can't learn everything. You just do what you can, do it in love, and stick by what you've done, 'cause the past will not return, and you won't get a redo.
Pathologic 2 dances with this idea beautifully.

Staying alive is a struggle, as the game makes use of very daunting survival mechanics and overbearing resource management, ensuring you can't just walk from marker to marker saving everyone. But, you're a doctor, it's your job to save everyone; moreso, you're the player, taught by years of gaming conventions to expect, and desire, to see every quest through to the end; but, as I said, it isn't so simple. The clock will continue to tick and the world will move on whether or not you choose to participate. And still your own survival must come first, for otherwise you won't save anyone anymore, meet anyone anymore. And to top it all off, to further get the point across of how your mistakes impede your life from ever being the same again, with each death you face, the game punishes you. I mean, really punishes you, permanently, as your deaths too become weaved into the more meta elements of the narrative. Load as many saves as you want, it still will not undo the damages. Your maximum health will be reduced, you'll become hungry faster, thirsty faster, tire way quicker, and no older saves from that specific run will be exempt of these handicaps. You expect to save everyone, but you can barely save yourself.

Save-scumming is still possible, though its reliability is minimal, and the game itself, along with the fandom, will vehemently recommend you don't. It's a game that encourages pushing forward with your mistakes and failures. Stick by them. Defends they make you stronger and better prepared, albeit not physically.

You'll learn to care for the people of the town and face every danger to keep them alive; you may even learn to love the town itself, as did I, with all its quirks and oddities, and seek to learn everything about it; but you cannot do it all. You must choose. At every instant, you're forced to make tough decisions, be they regarding your own interests or those of others, only to be reminded each and every time how these have now shaped your current reality, of which you can't escape, only adapt; almost all of this, through gameplay alone. Just as memorable as its story beats or lines of dialogue will be moments such as when you, during normal non-scripted gameplay, find yourself forced to sell your gun, which you toiled so hard to purchase, just so you can buy a piece of bread. Or when you manage to cure a friend instead of having them disappear from the game forever, along with every possible quest or conversation they may have still had in store. Yes, if a character dies on, say, day four of the twelve-day total, so does any chance of you finishing, or triggering, any of the other fantastic moments you could still have had with them. The devs and writers made them with such care... But fate had you miss them. Everything is missable.

If, like me, you're a gamer who seeks to see at least most of what a game has to offer, then I urge you to not interpret my previous paragraphs as reasons to steer clear, but as the opposite. That is what'll allow you to get the most out of the experience.
It'll make you frustrated. Your sensibilities will be in a constant clash with those of the game, and that's a good thing. That's what you want out of this. More than for its exceptional, top-notch, legitimately perfect gameplay loop, Pathologic 2 should be experienced for the ocean of ideas and philosohies it tries and succeeds in sharing, both through direct and indirect means. The writing is stunning, and far more poetic than what's expected of the medium, and the plot and characters are all up there as perhaps the best that gaming has to offer; but its true beauty only reveals itself after realizing how much of it you missed, how much you couldn't do, which will then provide you with a larger sense of accomplishment and attachment for all the things you did manage. The failure is unwashable but those successes are what keep you clean.

What results is a game that most agree isn't fun, but something else. Something more. If you're not yet convinced to try this absolutely exceptional work of art, high art, adamant on pushing games forward and treating them with more respect than most of its contemporaries, then I don't know what else to tell you. You're priving yourself of what'll likely be a most memorable and impactful experience, if only you choose to meet it at its level and go where it takes you--which is why I can't recommend enough thay you DON'T play it in one of the easier difficulties on your first run. It's meant to be hard enough that standing still is the most stressful thing you can do, and simply walking becomes enough of a challenge to warrant taking up most of your time (ie. Death Stranding). Do not prive yourself of that. If you see there's no way you can finish it under those conditions, then sure, but at least try, 'cause that first playthrough is something you'll never get back.

I know I'll replay it at some point, likely soon. I'm already itching to return to its streets and back-alleys. To breathe in its stunning art direction, accompanied by nothing but the town's sounds and the sound of my own thoughts. I want to learn more of it, specifically 'cause there's nothing quite like it. I want more.

I must admit, when I first tried the original "Pathologic," it struck me as a strange indie project, and I quickly abandoned it. Later, after reading enthusiastic reviews, I promised myself I'd revisit it but never found the time. Now I've had the opportunity to play "Pathologic 2," which is presented as a full reimagining of one of the original game's three storylines. Having completed it fully, I'd eagerly dive into the remaining two-thirds if they become available.

It's no big spoiler to reveal that the game unfolds in a remote steppe town gripped by a terrifying pandemic. The disease is unknown, spreads through airborne droplets, ravages the body swiftly, and proves fatal within a day. Although the town supposedly houses tens of thousands of residents, this is visually understated—just one of many gaming conventions. Among the population are dozens of significant characters with whom you interact extensively.

The protagonist must constantly manage hunger, thirst, immunity, exhaustion, and health. The core gameplay revolves around survival amidst extreme resource scarcity, especially time. Time moves inexorably forward, compelling you to make painful decisions since completing everything you wish is physically impossible. The town itself is a maze that changes daily, with barricades and obstacles emerging regularly. Losing precious time by taking a wrong turn is frustrating, often prompting a reload, though saving is restricted to specific locations. The narrative spans eleven in-game days (excluding the twelfth day), and with each passing day, time moves faster! This relentless pace ensures you're never truly at ease. Interestingly, the game allows you to bypass plot tasks entirely—provided you have sufficient food and water, you could theoretically sleep through to the ending. This isn't an oversight but another intentional design choice, reminding players they aren't always the central hero capable of saving everyone.

The game's atmosphere is intensely grim. Your character, a surgeon, must practically apply his skills—saving lives through operations, dissecting bodies to study the disease, or selling organs on the black market to afford basic sustenance. The agonizing infected are visually and audibly disturbing, and townsfolk gradually descend into madness, escalating from knife fights to burning people alive in desperate attempts to halt the epidemic.

Additional immersive elements include crafting items, repairing mechanisms, sewing clothes, sharpening weapons, and brewing medicines. There's also a distinctive mini-game for diagnosing illnesses and prescribing treatments. Though depicted simplistically, these elements add artistic charm.

However, not all mechanics were to my liking. Inventory management is particularly cumbersome. The game features nearly a hundred items, initially seeming like useless junk, yet each can become crucial for repairs or trading. The limited inventory size necessitates meticulous planning and creating stashes near save points to avoid unnecessary losses.

Additionally, the artificial limitations on item durability are frustrating. Clothing logically offers disease protection, but it deteriorates far too rapidly, as does weaponry, breaking after a few uses.

Combat is disappointing as well, particularly enemy AI. Bandits stubbornly continue to attack bare-handed despite being shot at with a shotgun, lacking any instinct for self-preservation.

Story-wise, however, the game is genuinely captivating, blending detective elements with mysticism and surrealism. Merely surviving becomes secondary to understanding unfolding events, unraveling mysteries, and attempting to rescue beloved characters. Yet no one is safe: any narrative character can contract the disease, and medicines are scarce, particularly since the protagonist also requires treatment. The developers deliberately instill a sense of fatalism—for instance, achieving one specific accomplishment necessitates allowing a particularly cherished character to die.

Game rules change daily. Neighborhoods become infected, risking contamination upon any contact; starvation drives locals to violence; barricades arise, water sources vanish, and shops close, replaced by illegal stalls. Prices and even currency fluctuate abruptly, rendering accumulated wealth worthless. Children, the primary source of medicine trades, eventually disappear from the streets. These perpetual changes maintain continuous engagement.

Notably, the death mechanic uniquely complicates gameplay: each protagonist's demise applies various debuffs, making subsequent survival harder. After repeated deaths, the game offers a "deal with the devil" to remove all negative effects—at a significant and irreversible cost, even if you reload a save. My advice: avoid this deal until you've completed the game at least once.

The standout feature remains the narrative itself. Explicit explanations are rare, and nearly every dialogue introduces new mysteries and enigmas. Its atmosphere somewhat evokes "Twin Peaks," rich in metaphors and allusions found in texts, imagery, and environment design. Unfortunately, there’s hardly time for contemplation due to the constant urgency. Occasionally, the protagonist's thoughts manifest as dialogues with shadowy versions of other characters. The developers also daringly break the fourth wall, portraying events alternately as dreams or theatrical performances, casting the player as an actor playing the protagonist.

I've seen this game described as living through a Dostoyevski novel and I can really get behind that. This game is not fun or all that rewarding and the endings both left me unsatisfied and/or uncomfortable. But it manages to be so compelling with its atmosphere, story and characters that you just feel the need to press on and see it through to the end. 

Really though, just like Crime and Punishment, its greatest strength is as food for thought and the more you chew on that cud the more you get out of it. Yes, Crime and Punishment is a bleak novel about a law student who killed two people just to see if he could, but it shows its true colors once you start diving into it as a dialectic: [i]"This guy killed some ladies and now I have to watch him be a moody anxious wreck for hundreds of pages"[/i] turns to [i]"So Rodion isn't like the Great Men of History that he wanted to prove himself to be by killing those women, but if what makes those men stand out is that they could step over other people so long as they were furthering their agenda, what makes them so Great that their crimes get to be justified? Luzhin and Svidrigailov did just that and they're both monsters!"[/i] etc. etc.
The lack of a satisfaction in Pathologic 2 gnaws at you in the same way - the two true endings of the game are so polarized from each other that I can't imagine this not being purposeful. There is no "better" ending. You shouldn't be content, whichever ending you end up choosing. 
Pathologic 2 has messages and themes that it wants to communicate to you and it is willing and able to be both painfully blunt and subtle about it at the same time. This is a game about idealism and how ideologies of people in power are payed for with the lives of a nameless, faceless majority; it's about how desperation drives people to do horrible things; it's about the power of art and how it doesn't have to make you feel good to be important and worth your time-- I could blabber on about this for hours.

Pathologic 2 is built to punish and hurt you and force you to confront its themes and I really can't recommend trying it enough. Until the bitter end it kept finding ways to hurt me. After replaying it for the nocturnal ending (you *could* just load your save and see the other ending but this felt more in line with the spirit of the game) I'm finally uninstalling it from my computer, but I suspect Pathologic 2 will be haunting me for a long time.

This game probably broke something in my brain. Try as I might, I really can't think of a game that has eaten my brain quite like this one (and the game it is a re-telling of), and I think that the amount of time I've spent in this game could probably be used as a diagnostic criteria for something. 

Although only one route is currently out (along with a short story from the Bachelor's perspective) and some aspects to the story are not fully explored as of yet, it is still complete and satisfying, and you don't necessarily need to have played Pathologic Classic in order to understand it, although I highly recommend playing it at some if you haven't already (either before or after this one). 

The Haruspex's route is about life, death, survival, and sacrifice, as one might expect, but it's also about family, love, belonging, rejection, time, childhood, adulthood, duty, and the devastating effects of settler colonialism, among other things. The story is unique, surreal, and engaging, and something you can dissect from multiple angles over and over again, extracting more from it each time. 

None of the characters in this game are normal. Everyone is interesting and at least somewhat strange in their own right, just like the setting. Artemy is a character that can be played in multiple ways, as many aspects of Artemy's character are meant to be in conflict with each other. It feels realistic for someone attempting to find one's place after a period of estrangement from their community and while trying to mend things that were broken, especially during a time of crisis. 

I wouldn't necessarily call it a "horror" game, but it is certainly unnerving and anxiety-inducing at points. The choices posed are difficult, and the evolving and unforgiving gameplay accentuates the struggle for survival against seemingly impossible odds. You can adjust the difficulty, but it's intended difficulty can be pretty grueling on a first time playthrough. However, the game walks you through the mechanics with straightforward tutorials and has a mind map that helps point you in the right directions, which sets it apart from its predecessor. This game also allows you to heal when you sleep, unlike Pathologic Classic, so that's also helpful. 

The only issue I'd say the game has is that it's not very well-optimized at times, and if you're playing it on a hard drive, you'll experience long wait-time lags at transitions between indoor and outdoor environments and loading screens. Using an SSD will reduce this issue significantly. I'm able to play it at max graphics settings on a gaming laptop that's relatively average specs-wise and get 30 FPS, which is fine by me, but your mileage may vary if you feel like a game running at anything but 60 FPS is unplayable. 

Some people might complain about the combat being difficult (although you can get into the rhythm of it if you practice enough), but I'd argue that fighting people in real life tends to be very high risk and sometimes the only reward is coming out out of it alive. However, unlike real life, you only really take a hit to your reputation if you decide to steal someone's liver - to make medicine, of course. 

Overall, it's a fantastic game. I'm waiting excitedly (but patiently, as the team is pretty small) for the next route.

[u] Quick notes: [/u]
1. If the rumored difficulty of Pathologic 2 is putting you off from buying/playing it, please disregard what you've heard. I've had this game in my backlog for 5 years and I'm so glad that I've finally played it. Yes, this game is full of suffering and no-win situations, but I didn't find the gameplay itself to be half as miserable or stressful as I'd feared. Just jump in, alright?
2. The intended difficulty can be tough at times, but it is also entirely manageable. Pre-plan your daily routes, collect herbs, hoard water, avoid fights, and avoid looting in infected/burnt buildings. Stealth and back alleys are your best friends for avoiding fights, and the time spent looting in dangerous districts is much better spent on quests--especially in the late game.
3. You can't complete every quest. You must decide what seems worth pursuing. There is no wrong answer.
4. You can't save everyone. This is a necessary part of the experience.

[u] Criticisms: [/u]
1. I had a few deaths that seemed to be bug related (I went to sleep and got a dream sequence, finished the dream, took damage from exhaustion while still on the sleep menu, and died?). The death penalties are real, but death is generally easy to avoid so long as you avoid the temptation to linger in infected/burnt districts. I didn't die enough times for the death penalties to be of significant consequence.
2. Aggressive frame drops in interiors...sporadically. It did not seem to be a function of specific interiors, length of a play session, etc. I'd recommend avoiding infected/burnt houses for this exact reason. Frames were very stable outdoors.
3. You can't pet the Wonder Bull and this makes me sad. 

Overall, I'd replay Pathologic 2 in a heartbeat, but other games are calling out for me. Anyway, I'm going to go boot up Pathologic Classic for some stress relief. See y'all later!

Murders, slaughter, looting, a plague that decimates the entire town, corpses, mass graves, war, deception, dead babies, hangings—this is all present in Pathologic 2, and even more horrifying stuff! 

The rules of this world are brutal and complex, punishing the player for even the slightest moment of negligence. Money, inflation, thirst and the search for food will be a constant problem. Should you break into a house and steal a piece of bread, risking the life of a household member or your own? Should you trade your so important tools with children for a boiled egg, just so you could survive for little while? Planning your route to avoid bandits and infected areas of the town will add pressure to save as many people from the plague as possible, with time running out. If hunger overwhelms you, or you get killed by a bandit or plague, the game punishes you for your death, complicating the rest of your playthrough without the option to reload without consequences (the penalty remains for all previous saves) or taking something unessential for your progress, but important for you (like the ability to hug someone). 

Chance to lose the ability to hug someone, and a feeling of dread after learning that you can't do that anymore, is the power of Pathologic 2, because it makes you care for its characters.

Beneath all this nightmare, lies an innocence and warmth that can only exist in a child's mind, or some kind of children's game. A polyhedron defying gravity, inhabited solely by children; a mountain-sized bull named Bos Turokh; Characters that look like villains but are actually gentle and good; worm-people; time travel, prophet rats, ghosts...

This conflict between the rational and irrational horror, and the world of childhood, warmth, and the possibility of change and growth, makes the world of Pathologic 2 so convincing and real! Its brutality in gameplay is justified by the tenderness it shows towards its characters. As a haruspax, a surgeon, you, the player, genuinely want to save these people from the plague. You want to save them all. At first, you don't even know why, because the game draws you into its magic so quickly. It compels you to believe in it.

No matter how hard you fight, or what choice you make when it comes to that (and in the end, a tough choice awaits you), you can’t save everyone. And the game teaches you that. And it hurts.

And you will always be plagued by the thought that you're doing something wrong, you just don't know what.

[i]Unique.

Adjective: being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else.
Particularly remarkable, special, or unusual.
Belonging or connected to one particular person, group, or place.

.....

"Belonging or connected".....

Connections.... Lines.... 

"Emshen"... He who sees the Lines... Draws the Lines... Makes connections.[/i]

.

When I started Pathologic 2, I thought I was playing the role of the character Artemy Burakh, and I took for granted the notion that this was a "role-playing game", and could affect a certain level of control over the world I was inhabiting by means of the choices I made--choices that were, as a surgeon, very literally matters of life and death... But eventually, I learned that even a doctor administering treatment to the sick (though he may very well determine whether his patient lives or dies) is still subject to the [i]Lines.
 
.

A line is a path, a direction, a singular course. From past to future, from here to there...

A line connects all points having a specified common property

A line is the precise demarcation of a boundary, a notional limit, a way of thinking...[/i]

.

He performs surgery by the very act of cutting [i]Lines[/i] into a body: Should he perform his Lines well, he will be known to the Steppe folk as [i]Emshen[/i]--"Knower of Lines"--or he can (both literally and figuratively) [i]butcher them[/i]. The Steppe folk have a word for this too: [i]Yargachin[/i]. It designates Artemy by his profession as a surgeon, but the word also means "butcher", as in, someone who simply cuts up the meat of a living being. And so the the distinction is made between cutting haphazardly into meat and performing surgery.
 
[i]A Line is drawn.[/i]

It's not an accident that the word chosen to refer the player's path (i.e. the [i]Line[/i] one follows through the unfolding of events)--is the very same word used to refer to an actor's dialogue within a theatrical production.

It turns out that Pathologic 2 is indeed a role-playing game, but only in the same way that an actor in a stage production also [i]plays a role[/i]: He has no real say in the unfolding of the events of the play, nor even in his own part therein, but he is nonetheless given the opportunity to embody the character and give expression to his part.

[i]Try not to butcher your Lines, Yargachin...[/i]

This, ultimately, is the lesson of Pathologic 2. In fact, this is the explicitly-stated philosophical underpinning of the entire game. The developers even tell you this directly through the fourth wall, via the character of Mark Immortell, the stage director. He literally tells you these things to your face--repeatedly, in fact, every time you die--but it wasn't until I had already sunk several dozen hours into the game before I fully considered the scope of what his words meant: that no matter what I did or what I said, the outcome would always be the same; that although I could not [i]overcome[/i] death, or [i]transcend[/i] it, I could [i]achieve mastery over it.[/i] The difference between performing surgery and cutting haphazardly into meat. 

[i].

He who follows the Lines needs not know of their existence; his path is still preordained.

The play remains the same. The role of an actor remains the same.
 
All he can do... is know the Lines.[/i]

.

Initially, I was disappointed with the lack of agency I had while playing, particularly when it came to dialogue interactions. I would save, enter into dialogue with a character, and come out of the interaction feeling like the choices I had made and the things I had said had produced a tangible outcome in the world. But when I would reload my file, re-enter the same conversation, and choose different dialogue options, I would [i]produce the exact same outcome[/i]. It bothered me that what we said to each other ultimately had no effect on what we did. It felt like what would otherwise be a source of agency, or even a system to be gamed in order to produce a desired outcome, was actually completely ineffectual.

Upon reflection, I'm not sure this is such a bad thing... Much of the game seems poised to instill a sense of futility; why should the dialogue sequences be any different? After all, the people who inhabit the world of Pathologic lie to you and mislead you and distract you with all kinds of wild goose chases and false promises.... So why should I believe that anything I could say could really make a difference here? Maybe this is the developer's commentary on the emptiness of words and the primacy of action; a slap in the face of players who believed that they could simply achieve their goals by assembling the right combination of utterances, the fools (like me) who tried to phrasemonger themselves into a happy ending...

It is through painstaking realizations such as this that Pathologic forces everyone it comes into contact with to re-evaluate their preconceived notions of what it means to play a video game.

[i]What even is a game?[/i]
 
At its most fundamental level, a game is just a closed system of variables with which players can interact in order to achieve a win state. Pathologic 2 fulfills this description, of course, but it is [i]so[/i] much more than that. On the surface, the system of variables that Pathologic employs are primarily immersive sim-style survival mechanics: Your character needs to eat, sleep, and take medicine when sick. This system is absolutely "gamed", but it is also simultaneously working on a deeper level: Pathologic uses these game elements as vehicles to force the player into simulating extreme, even apocalyptic survival situations. The moral weight of these situations are treated with an incredible level of acuity: Questions of the soul, morality, violence, trauma, desperation, perseverance, authority, truth... these are the real preoccupations of Pathologic 2.

I know what you're thinking: A walking simulator that's more concerned with getting the player to philosophize than to actually play a game sounds heavy-handed and pretentious as hell.
 
[i]But it isn't.[/i]
 
The game isn't pretentious, or pompous, or blowing hot air. Not even a little bit. In fact, much the opposite. It is frequently tongue-in-cheek, and well aware of its own absurdity. It asks only that the player make decisions and then deal with the consequences... or, worse yet, to reckon with the fact that the decisions they made had absolutely no effect whatsoever on the outcome.

I'm finalizing this review on the 10th of July, 2024--a full year after having last played Pathologic 2. And yet, I continue to think about this game. I'm writing this right now because, even 12 months later, I [i]can't help[/i] but think about it. It is completely unlike anything else within the gaming world, whether digital or tabletop, and has left an indelible mark upon me. Pathologic 2 is a work of art. It elevates video gaming as a form. 

It is completely unequaled in the world of video games for a work to be so high-minded and philosophically ambitious; to directly inform the player of its lofty goals through the fourth wall, and then achieve said goals in spectacular fashion.
 
Pathologic 2 is totally distinct among its peers.

A singular experience.

Every once in a while, you find through the medium of games some works that go beyond mere "games" and Pathologic 2 is definitely one of them. It is the type of interactive media that manages to bring forth the most beautiful concept of art, which is the capacity to evoke the most profound and primal emotions of the human psyche. All of this is achieved while building a whole living and breathing fictional universe through its attention to detail in the story, the universe, the characters, the mythology, the visuals, and the music. Here lies the beauty of Pathologic 2: its immersiveness and detailed universe, with a whole fictional culture, language and mythology of its own.

I won't delve deeply into the gameplay/survival mechanics and the lore of the game overall, since it's [b]REALLY RECOMMENDED[/b] to dive into this game completely blind and on the Imago Difficulty (the intended difficulty) to truly feel what the game wants you to experience. However, it is easy to say that the game breaks many genre staples and is punitive, putting you in the most uncomfortable and anxiety-inducing situations. You will probably fail many times, and that's completely fine and entirely intended. Pathologic 2 is a game with a very direct and solid philosophy envisioned by the developers. In true Russian literature fashion, it's a game about the tragedy of life, accepting and overcoming death and suffering. It's a game where defeat and loss are inherent to its gameplay, wanting you to accept and overcome all the imperfections, mistakes, and sacrifices so you can still manage to survive the next day. The game lets you learn by experience that you are not the perfect hero; you [b]CANNOT CONTROL EVERYTHING[/b], you [b]CANNOT SAVE EVERYONE[/b], and you [b]DON'T HAVE THE TIME[/b] to do everything. You will have to make choices and sacrifices that will affect important aspects of the whole game, such as characters and your own experience as the player. This philosophy permeates every aspect of the game. Pathologic 2 it's not a game you play, it's a game you go to war with.

It's difficulty is really overstated. it's really just about changing your mindset compared to how you would usually play a game.

This game pressures you a lot into thinking you have a lot of choices, especially with how the journal is laid out, but it's one of those games where your choices kind of really don't matter and everything will end up the same regardless of what you do. There is only one decision that truly matters and that's the one for which ending you will get. 

Once you do a first full playthrough, a second one will be laughably easy as you will know what you will need to do to "win" the game which is making sure none of the main characters die so you get access to all of their content and quests.
 
Going back on the endings... They are very underwhelming though. Compared to the very cinematic first few minutes of the game, it's clear the budget hit the floor for the last 2 days of the game, felt very rushed and unpolished in comparison.

Otherwise, it's a very immersive experience. No game has really made me feel a sense of doom before. Easily a top 10 game for me despite my complaints.

Pathologic 2 is a reimagining of the horror-survival game Pathologic. The point of Pathologic (2) is not to feed your ego. Really, it perhaps can only be accurately described as starving you, your ego, and your empathy. Because the point of Pathologic 2 is different from other games, even within the survival genre. It wishes to challenge you, the player, to engage with a game that is so outside of the realm of anything you have experienced that it is as foreign as the setting itself.

If you have no experience with survival games in any fashion, this will be a wild ride unlike any game you have ever played- and likely will ever play after.

Once you've booted up Pathologic 2 you may see a funny little button placed within the settings, a 'difficulty' bar. This is automatically set to 'Intended difficulty'  and requires flipping off before you can see a detailed breakdown of all of the literal torture devices the game has crafted for you. Because this isn't just a game about surviving a thirst and exhaustion bar, only to eventually and inevitably become the king of the wilderness; this is a game where there are only bad options and you will never, and I do mean never, be a morally upright hero. 

You are literally playing a doctor turned ripper. A 'menkhu' that cuts and cuts. No matter what you do, you become a murderer through and through.

Without spoiling the incredible story in any other way because it has to be experienced yourself, this game is worth playing for the narrative alone. Your main motivation against such seemingly impossible odds as a plague in a town secluded from all other civilizations needs to be excellent, and the developers know it. There was no obstacle I wasn't ready to get my hands dirty for through barter, murder, theft, consumption, manipulation, or simply death in order to continue the story. 

It has a very theatrical feel to its story which is entirely intentional, so going into this game with the expectation that you're an actor on a stage will will serve you well. That doesn't make the dilemma any less human or agonizing, it may even make it worse.

Oh, and do remember, death is not the end of this particular play. You will almost assuredly die, and you will likely die more than once. Here's a piece of advice, don't bother reloading after death. The narrative becomes all the richer the more deaths you've... lived through. 

Though it is gritty and dark as is clearly an intentional choice visible from the art design and desaturated color scheme, it is also a surprisingly hopeful tale in the end, regardless of the ending you choose (unless you are late, so don't be late). After raking up nearly 63 hours myself over the course of just one playthrough and the DLC, which is nothing compared to some people's 200 hours spent with this game, clearly there is something special about it that really claws into some of us.

But something very important to note is that this is a sequel. The original game, simply 'Pathologic' which came out in 2005 holds within it two other stories which have not yet been implemented into this one. As it turns out, a real world plague happened (ironic) amongst other developmental problems, but the game as it currently stands is an entirely finished stand alone remake of the Haruspex experience from that game. If you want to play the others, the Bachelor and the Changeling, I highly recommend you do if you fall in love with this one. 

But, I must also warn you that it is even harder than this one. 

Please, if you are considering this game and any of this sounds interesting to you, give it a try. It runs sales quite often, so for only under $10 you could be playing a game that you will love. It won't be for everyone, especially if you know that you don't like failure, but if you do then this is the game you should have been shown a long time ago.

Ice Pick Lodge posits the bold question- just how fucked can one town be?

Pathologic 1 is almost certainly one of the best written games in history, held back purely by a lack of budget, polish, and some mediocre gameplay when it comes to interacting with the town. Pathologic 2, the sleeker and bolder successor is one of the greatest games of all time. Every moment spent in the town is steeped in feelings of anxiety, terror, despair, and most ephemerally, beauty. While the game retains the masterful writing of its predecessor (and fortunately commits to giving all characters an important role and oppurtunity to speak in the Haruspex route this time) I hesitate to mention how deep and well-thought this symphony of perspective is as it may cheapen the way the themes and ideas that creep up and consume the player from all angles.

What I would like to state clearly however is that this is perhaps the greatest example I have ever seen of games as art. Not games whose artistic voice is cinematic or theatric a la Metal Gear, or literary like basically every VN (bar totono), but engraining its message and voice through the laws that govern the world and the decisions you are allowed to make as a player. While the game is at all times cruel are very few times when the game is explicitly "unfair", which are given very clear voice and reason by the plot surrounding it. As such the player is engrossed in the role of Burakh and the decisions you make are legitimized by the honesty in not railroading the player in this or that way. Who you choose to save, who you must ignore, and what you say to influence future events are never really guided truly by the developer. In fact the developers wish instead that they could remove even their helping hand in taking away your guides and journals, but admit that such a degree of abandonment would probably make the art oblique to the point of being unplayable by most.

But beyond the mere freedom afforded the player the choices matter to a magnificent extent. When characters die they are truly gone, and the void they leave behind is palpable. Quests you do on one play-through could be entirely missing on another because you let the certain characters pass. Likewise you may choose the wrong dialogue choice and lose someone's trust for days, or prevent a shelter from being opened for the entire run. It's seriously something that must be played at least twice, not just for the ending but for a different perspective throughout. The interactive elements provide such a broad degree of the town where you can better understand everyone in it, it's something that could only be done in this medium.

And adding on top of that peak aesthetics and OST, some of the most memorable moments I've had in games, and just enough of that slavic artistic strangeness and you have an absolute masterpiece. It goes on sale for <$10 fairly often, you MUST pick this bad boy up. In theory the best way to experience it is by playing P1 first starting with Bachelor, but given its high barrier to entry I totally understand starting from here (as I did).

If they never release Bachelor route I will be very upset.

To save time, I'll summarize the experience I had with Pathologic 2 in bullet-points. These will cover points of contention I initially had with the game (and how they quickly turned into features which improved my experience) as well as the "best parts" of the game as a whole.

Learning Curve: I had Pathologic sitting inside of my library for nearly three months before I decided to play more than 30 minutes into the story. Before you gain an appreciation for the slow-burn timing of the game, it's going to feel somewhat agonizing. However, once you immerse yourself in the story and characters, you'll actually feel pressed on time: As though the world is moving too fast for you to keep up. Combat mechanics are straight forward but asset management takes some getting used to - The latter being essential to succeeding on a playthrough. 

Writing and Storytelling: Only second to *maybe* Disco Elysium and Knights of the Old Republic. Nothing short of fantastic, as long as you take your time to appreciate it. The story is *extremely flexible* too, with your actions having drastic consequences on the story depending on your dialogue options. What's unique about Pathologic 2, is that the consequences are *on-going* in the story, not something that arbitrarily effects a set-ending as in Disco E or KOTOR. You are altering the story, cover to cover. Also, the doesn't spell out important decisions or comments you make with obnoxious "persuasion check" or tacky coloring. Like all real-time conversations: Once it's out there, it's out there and you have no idea how it'll turn out.

Atmosphere: The game has aged amazing, given when it was made. The atmosphere can be terrifying and tranquil depending on where you are. Interactions with the characters will leave you with a sense of sonder - Craving more and more insight into who they are and what they might be thinking as they interact with you. You truly feel like an entity separate from the world around you. In the best way possible: You feel utterly out of control and helpless. More playtime rewards you with a lessened sense of helplessness, encouraging you to master the game and your playthroughs.

Overall, the game stands as one of the best titles I've ever had the pleasure of experiencing. A great gift and recommendation to people who enjoy storytelling and crave that feeling of emptiness upon completing a game. A feeling which beckons you back, again and again, because you know there's nothing quite like it out there.

Pathologic 2 is a remake, in a manner of speaking, of Pathologic.

Anyway. Pathologic is a game where, as odd as it sounds, "having fun" is not the focus. The story is. The experience.
It's a bit tricky to explain what Pathologic truly is, but I find it to be wildly different from most games I've played.
While it ticks most boxes of an open world adventure RPG, it's one of the very few games where your actions will have actual, serious consequences for the world (or rather, town).

The manner you interact with your fellow man directly influences if you'll get anywhere. You're not a super hero, you're just a human, made of the same squishy, fragile matter as everyone else.
Which, of course, means that you will die of diseases just as much as everyone else. Or of hunger. Or thirst.
And if you make people upset, store owners will no longer trade with you. People will scorn you, and - in the worst case - actively try to hunt you down.

Oh, the lives of this town depend on you. The people aren't rational, they believe ancient stories, and the authorities, who ought to help you, will try to sabotage your work throughout.

Sounds like fun? Don't be so quick to toss the idea. I'd compare it to an interactive book (there's a lot of reading, still).

A Hauntingly Beautiful Survival Experience

Pathologic 2 has swiftly climbed the ranks to become one of my all-time favorite games. From the moment you step into its eerie, mist-laden rural town, you're enveloped in an atmosphere that's both vividly alive and tinged with an otherworldly fantasy feel. 

**Atmosphere and World-Building:**
The town itself is a character, teeming with a diverse array of inhabitants, each adding their unique flavor to this grim tapestry. Wandering through the grey, fog-draped streets is an experience in itself, where getting lost feels like part of the journey, enhancing the sense of a living, breathing world.

**Characters:**
The characters in Pathologic 2 are where the game truly shines. Notkin, Vlad, Grif, and many others are not just NPCs; they are complex, memorable individuals with stories that make you care about this doomed town. Each interaction feels meaningful, contributing to the overarching narrative.

**Gameplay:**
Gameplay in Pathologic 2 is intense and unforgiving, perfectly capturing the desperation of a plague-ridden dystopia. The freedom to explore and shape your character's path adds depth, allowing for a personalized experience where your decisions impact how others perceive and react to you. This lack of boundaries makes for a unique sandbox of survival and social dynamics.

**Story and Mechanics:**
While the main storyline might be linear, it's the urgency and the pacing that make every moment in the game feel critical. Time is a resource as precious as any in-game item, making you truly invest in the unfolding events. However, some might find character movement a bit stiff, and combat can be punishingly hard, but these are minor quibbles in an otherwise stellar experience.

**Visuals and Performance:**
The game's aesthetic contributes greatly to its atmosphere. 

**Conclusion:**
Pathologic 2 isn't just a game; it's an experience—a survival narrative. Despite its minor flaws, the game delivers an unparalleled atmospheric adventure. I'm eagerly hoping for a continuation, as I'm not ready to leave this captivating world behind. For anyone willing to dive into a challenging, narrative-driven survival game with a unique setting, Pathologic 2 comes highly recommended.

TLDR: Pathologic 2 is a game that wants to do 2 things. Show you a story in which there IS no big hero, least of all you. And to make you feel the unrelenting burden of testing your own survival against the survival of those around you. You need to give the game to the end of day 3 to get a sense for how things are going to be, and this WILL take you over the refund mark. Finally, you only get ONE first playthrough, dont cheat yourself by looking things up. This game is best experienced raw and uncut, anything less would be a disservice to yourself.

Pathologic 2, you've read a hundred times in the reviews that it is a pain simulator, and to a certain extent this is accurate. It is also, however, a fairly shallow explanation for the game. Since this part is no secret, you will be playing the part of a surgeon returning home at the onset of a plague, you will be pressed for time, resources, and ability to be able to even scratch the surface of being capable of helping anyone else much less yourself.

The game puts you in an alien world, one that you (the player) need to learn and you (the character [Artemy]) need to learn again, having only returned to the town just now after years away studying surgery. The beliefs of the local tribal culture as well as the local town have meshed and become something that the game wants you to feel like you need to learn from scratch. While yes, the game is tutorializing you on things by telling you all this, its doing so to remind you that you (the player and the character) are just shy of an outsider again, you need to learn how to live here again.

The game is hard, it tells you from the outset that the journey is lessened by the lack of failure.  You aren't expected to be perfect, you arent expected to be a hero, you arent expected to save everyone .... or for that matter ANYONE but yourself! After all, what good is a surgeon whos dead? After how is one person (Well ... technically 3, youll get it pretty quick) supposed to stop a force of nature the like of which legitimately had the whole of Europe and Asia in a chokehold during the same general timeframe?! And who are you to even think you CAN do anything to stop it?

There are themes of spiritual happenings, as well as some supernatural themes. The world loves metaphors and will often times speak to you with exclusively those. Dont worry though, the one thing that will stop the inevitable march of time is dialogue, so take what time you need to unravel the things being talked about and how you respond to them, lives may be at stake with the simple misunderstanding of a dialogue.

And lastly, this is a personal thing, I like rogue likes. And while the reason i bring this up is likely not readily apparent, it becomes more so apparent when you know that the game CAN and WILL kill off any character you fail to properly care for, as well as those you do, assuming fate is not on your side. It will patch holes to some extent if characters are missing, but sometimes the reality is certain things just DONT WORK when someone is dead. You cant finish a quest to get some bread from the baker if the baker and their entire city block has been tossed on the communal corpse pyre! And there are certain things you can miss that will outright seal the fate of the town one direction or the other. The game WILL NOT pull punches, and your only chance is to look at the world objectively and try to decide what is the most important, who can do the most good. Remember the setting, remember past interactions, consult your mind map, the right choice may not always be the first one that comes to mind.

This game is fantastic in a way that I am, frankly, not eloquent enough to explain without illiciting actual spoilers. And I think that also is telling to how great it is. I said this in the tldr, but i feel anyone reading this far into as poorly structured of a review as this should hear it again, because I believe you're probably already convinced by something else. You only get ONE first run of Pathologic 2, the story if wonderful and worth replaying, but you will only get that raw visceral feeling of the consequences of your direct actions against the plague ONCE. I beg of you, do not cheat yourself out of that experience! There will of course be mechanics you may need explained, any of course knowing HOW to play is one thing. But do NOT seek answers to the riddle until you have tried to solve it to its end first! Dont savescum (no judgement, i do it too) to save that character you empathize with or undo that choice you didnt realize would have that effect. Live out your first run start to finish and accept what fate gives you as you struggle to push it in the direction you want to see. And I hope, like me. That you feel that you've done all you could, saved all that you could save, lost all you can afford to lose. After all, you were warned from the very beginning, wern't you?

If I have to stop playing to attend something else, the game expects me to keep my computer on and wasting energy for hours on end just so I don't lose progress? Ridiculous. A limited-save system to add difficulty makes sense for games where you complete one level at a time (fail the challenge and you're punished by having to waste time, e.g. Dark Souls), but for an open-ended game, where you can't predict how much time the player will waste, it's simply inexcusable.

At this point, I sadly can't recommend buying Pathologic 2. 

- The game is plagued by performance issues (the framerate fluctuates wildly between 144 and as low as sub 30 for no apparent reason and it is spiking both my CPU and GPU temps to unreasonable levels).

- It's 2019 and apparently developers still make games with hardcoded keybindings, making it a pain to play on anything but the default WASD setup (the developers have stated that they will try to address this in a future patch). In addition to that, the game has controller prompts showing up in the keybinding menu, even though the game itself has no controller support whatsoever (Although it had controller support in the demo, so it might get added back in for the full game at some point).

- The atmosphere suffers greatly from stiff (and sometimes completely non-existent) animations. For example, turning on "crouch" simply dims the edges of your screen, but your character does not actually crouch.

- The game currently suffers from gamebreaking bugs, one of which I have encountered myself already and would require me to re-play about 40+ minutes of the intro.

The game seems like it has the potential to be a great atmospheric thriller in an interesting quirky world, but until the above-mentioned issues are resolved, it's unfortunately not an enjoyable experience to play.

[list]
    [*]Whenever I play a game I, if I have to ASK MYSELF WHY I’M PLAYING THIS GAME I stop and try to figure out why and I’ve never  continued a game when that question is asked, so this review will be my thoughts after that question popped in my head

    [*]I’ve NEVER PLAYED THE FIRST ONE and heard this game is weird, has harsh survival and cool mechanics tied being limited time and you can’t do everything in the game to figure out what is going on and this premise appealed to me, as unique games are what I always want to try and I will say the vibe is good and can see why it has a cult following, but I just couldn’t find myself to enjoy it or even know what I’m getting out of playing it.

But one of the reasons the story failed to grasp me it how obtuse everything is, this isn’t like Dark souls where the lore is hidden and you need to find where to look to get it, here it feels like they are talking gibberish or some cryptic poems that I don’t know what is being said and my mind wanders, the way the story is told is just too out for me to pay attention or care to put the effort to find out if it gets better.

Combat is also forgivingly described as...clunky. Like, I get it, you're some mook that isn't a judo master...but the fights are a combination of hitbox and swing timing/animation frustration, and I expect them to only get more frequent as time goes on.

Pathologic 2 is an interesting survival, mystery, horror game that lets you explore a large town and figure out the disturbance in the area. The game is beautiful, and plot is aplenty. However, if you're not a fan of walking simulators, or survival, you're gonna have a bad time. Resources are scarce, and lots of trading is done by bartering; swapping items. There is still money for shops, but there is a lot more bartering. There is a day and night cycle, and fast travel is only available by using a scarce resource, so with the very limited time you have available, you will find yourself walking around - a lot. This is, of course, a survival game, so you have a hunger bar, health, infection, and tiredness bar, which goes low very quickly. You also have an influence / relationship bar with the many sections of the town, where you start very low, and people will randomly attack you, mobbing you to death. Don't think about fighting back though, otherwise your influence will drop lower, and you'll get mobbed more often. With very little save spots, walking endlessly, and it being a survival game, you will find yourself very dying often; survival is fun huh? Honestly, if it wasn't for the survival aspect (or if it was toned down at least), and you can travel around easier, and there were more saves, this would be a great game.

[i]Preamble (added for clarification): Liking Pathologic 2 is completely legit. This game was simply too hard to recommend for me. This is a review about why so many people like it expressly for the reasons that make it hard to enjoy. Please stay respectful and read at your own discretion.[/i]
----
This is more of an artistic experience than a game, and therefore the perfect example of critics contrasting the average consumers. I think this game is fantastic; but not as a game, and certainly not for most, hence [b]I do not recommend by default[/b]. The braveness of direction and design earns its laudatio, but it is hell to play. Very hard to describe. If you enjoy this, you are probably pathologic.

I dropped the game, twice. (Edited again for clarification.) I kinda hated playing it. Following others' advice, I played to the 2-3hr mark and since it didn't click for me by that point, it likely wouldn't ever since the rest of the game doesn't change. In order to understand the positive reviews I consumed hella deep dive YouTube content on it, so [h3]here is my analysis on why reviews are [i]raving so hard they could be a club in Berlin[/i] whereas actual gamer completion rates for Pathologic games are low.[/h3]

1. As most reviews will tell you, this is an incredibly niche experience for a hyperspecific kind of people. Namely, theatre-minded (not general art, specifically stage plays) folks who vibe with cryptic weirdness and anarchic breaking of styles and conventions, even when resulting in inaccessibility for a general populace. Literally the entire appeal of this game is its [i]performance[/i] - not a literal benchmark, but a performance of pathos and meta breaking. A lot of Pathologic analysis YouTubers also did stuff on mindbending shows like Neon Genesis Evangelion or Utena, if you care for comparisons. Which means the target audience for this is not gamers, but a theatrical audience that is looking [b]to be played instead of to play[/b]. You can't be good at Pathologic. You cannot get better at Pathologic. You can not enjoy Pathologic as a game in its most fundamental, ludic sense. It forces you to give up control. If you're in this cerebral niche, you will love this game all the more and 100% write a review on it; hence the amount of raving reviews not being proportional to the amount of players actually playing the game. And that is fine. Liking Pathologic is fine, but it is also niche.

2. Pathologic 2 has amazing narrative direction moving between layers of player consciousness, that however also requires a high cognitive investment and intrinsic motivation to actively want to experience that. The gameplay is neither rewarding nor good. Saying that it's not good (it's extremely punishing and slow-paced) does not negate the fact the game can still be good for people who weren't looking for that in this game anyways. Saying that this game design being 100% intentional does not negate the fact it will still drive away most people, understandably so. People expect different things out of games, e.g. not going through an existential crisis and not sitting through a performance. I'm not talking about the story or philosophy, but the literal gameplay (or rather, its intrinsic and unbearable dependance on story hooks to keep players tolerating it).

3. Pathologic is one of the most unique "games" out there. However, all prior points combined, in order to acquire its unique writing one has to go through such sluggish, stressful gameplay that it should be understandable when people don't like it, it doesn't mean they didn't try to like it or didn't understand the game. The more you like Pathologic, the more you will agree it is not a game meant to be played as a game, and therefore scare off most.

4. Lastly, a ton of comparisons to classic Russian existentialist and/or nihilist literature are drawn in comments and reviews. I will end by saying that the people who enjoy this game would probably all enjoy Dostoyevsky, but not all who enjoy Dostoyevsky will enjoy this game - and that is fine. I'd rather someone drop it respectfully than anybody being disrespectful about others "not getting it".

[i]Pathologic 2[/i] is one of the worst games I've ever played. That probably sounds like over-dramatic hyperbole, but I mean it: Its' failings are chronic and profound; worse, the reason is, I believe, that these failings are intentional. The developers have taken a wrong path in their journey through life, such that they have misunderstood game-design so badly that [i]Pathologic 2[/i] intentionally and systematically is structured to be the worst possible game it could manage to be.

It's a long-form campaign, time-limited game with a single save-slot - you can play the game for a long time, then discover you're in a position from which you cannot progress effectively, and thus be expected to begin afresh to replay over from scratch. That might be something I'd call a bold, impressive design-decision, demanding of its player, except that every part of the plot is so alienating, and the game-play so boring and slow. The plot takes an abstract, surrealist approach, plunging the player into the midst of weird inexplicability over and over. All well and good: But it does so with wandering talkiness, dialogue after dialogue of incoherent, rambling, context-free nonsense. There are NPCs all over the place to interact with, and eventually I just stopped bothering, because I was sick to death of being bored witless by reading (and it is reading, since it isn't a voice-acted game) the directionless babble and selecting from dialogue trees where each option was equally meaningless to me (whatever meaning it might have to the player-character).

The intro-section of the game is long, alienating and functionally pointless - choking the player on obscurity without raising story-questions to capture interest due to sheer lack of context to give it any ground - it's just one long chain of metaphorical provocations. This at least has the dubious merit that it sets out the game's stall to make the player aware how the rest of the game will be - symbolism that is symbolic of nothing. And it doesn't even manage to do the simple intro-task of a proper interface-tutorial: After I'd finally begun what I judged to be the real game (which is where the intro should have begun, had I been designing the game), one of the first things I did was to accidentally murder a patient I was performing surgery on by extracting his liver for my own private collection (or to eat?).  

Together, these aspects reminded me somewhat of [i]The Void[/i], another game in the same 'intentionally bad' mould, except without the otherworldly landscapes, semi-nude girls, bright colour-contrasts and Hellraiser-esque character-designs to please the eye visually: [i]Pathologic 2[/i] is a traditional 'misery-brown' colour-scheme game. 

But there's more. Foolishly for a game so surreal and abstract, it takes the approach of feeding what passes for its story (i.e. its metaphorical provocations and gibberish dialogue) in a continual "tell-don't-show" pattern, instead of letting the player find it all for themselves emergently in the environment, in visual conceits - it's droned into you from the NPCs instead, and just to really lampshade that the game features 'Reflections' and 'Prompters' the NPCs that look like white-masked mime or traditional Chinese-ghost images, whose entire role is just to do that - to talk (in suggestive hints) about the symbolism of the part of the environment you're standing in, or to tell the player what the real character and motivations of the main NPCS are (the character you've just been talking to feels this, is like that, and wants that - just in case you can't draw your own inferences about the character from having had the damned dialogue with them yourself to begin with) - it is storytelling at its' most incompetent. 

And game-play itself is clearly designed to be as intentionally obscure and alienating as possible as well. Objectives are presented in an intentionally confusing way, as 'Thoughts', diagrams of nodes linked together with no ranking of significance, so as to simulate real mental flexibility and abstract ordering of ideas? It means the player has no feeling of progress or advancement as they play - it's all side-quest, and with no goal-and-reward for each side-quest to prompt further play. Open-world mechanics like people randomly attacking you when you're in a territory where you have a low popularity rating have no safety-valve to give the player any sense of control or meaning - you get attacked, get the hell beaten out of you by 5 enemies (because the combat is a very high challenge-level, also), and collapse, then regain consciousness a short distance away - but you're still in that area, and still have the same side-quest markers on the map you're supposed to be trying to reach, so what is there to do but to start walking toward them again through the same unpopular territory (and there is usually only 1-2 ways to approach any particular goal, as it's one of those first-person-in-a-refrigerator-box games where it walls off places the player is not meant to enter by just forbidding the player from climbing over chest-high fences/squeeze past a stack of boxes etc.), so that the exact same thing happens again - and again. 

There's other, pettier stuff that annoyed the hell out of me, that I would have forgiven in other games - hangs for loading times and unnecessary delays while making interface selections, etc. In [i]Pathologic 2[/i] it combined with the failures of its overall design to provoke me to loathing and disgust. 

I cannot recommend heartily enough that you do not waste your money, time or mental energies on this valueless trash.

Pathologic 2, at the time of this review, has one route out of three published. This means the Haruspex's route must stand alone, while simultaneously convincing players to be interested in the upcoming routes. Unfortunately, if you look past the survival mechanics that occupy most of the player's time, it comprehensively fails to deliver on its fancy narrative themes or give its characters depth.

The first thing the game tells you is that Pathologic 2 is literally a play in which the player is the main actor and the audience. A corollary is that the other NPCs are just there for your benefit, and aren't working towards their own goals. The two competing healers don't do anything to hinder you (besides give you quests), and many, many other characters' arcs have been rewritten to focus on the Haruspex, breaking the motivations that made them well-written in the original. This is perhaps most apparent in the fact that there are no factions: the player is tasked with caring for every person in the town, for no other reason than "his father told him to watch out for a list of kids", but the future of the Town has nothing to do with those people.

Everything revolves around the Haruspex, and yet nobody will tell you anything. There's a constant stream of "go away, we're having an important conversation that doesn't involve you", with occasional deep-sounding vagaries about fate and puppetry. This is intended to keep you interested in the upcoming routes, but frustrates the route's ability to stand on its own. Characters frequently say the Haruspex is too stupid to understand their activities, which falls short of being a running joke and becomes deeply uncomfortable given that he's the game's only Indigenous PC. At the same time, you can meet characters' "Reflections" that tell you the NPCs' innermost feelings, which a) stops the game from ever showing these feelings through actions, and b) limits their characterization for the upcoming routes.

Pathologic 2 has received wide acclaim in gaming journalism for its high-concept themes. (For the record, this constant praise let the lead writer fly under the radar as a child groomer for years). But the theme receiving the most attention- the Haruspex's mixed Indigenous identity- is explored through a shockingly racist set of quests (it's revealed that [spoiler]the Kin aren't harmed by the plague because they're a mindless, faceless mass who don't think for themselves[/spoiler]), and ends with a binary choice that completely fails to accomplish what both the antagonist and the director tell you was the point of the game: [spoiler]the Haruspex is meant to connect the Town and Kin, but the actual choice is which one of them you want to kill[/spoiler].

The other big theme is the meta of characters' fate being set within the video game, and leads to what I think is its best concept: an ending where [spoiler]you reject your part in the game and leave the Town to journey with your companion, a personification of Death, forever[/spoiler]. However, despite the game's insistence that "you have to break your fate to become truly human," this is framed as unequivocally the worst thing you could do! The game contradicts itself on both of its thematic selling points, and never offers the player an appropriate narrative conclusion.

Death itself is a core topic in Pathologic, which is why this game's failure to incorporate it is so jarring. While almost any of the NPCs can die, none of their deaths affect the game whatsoever. In contrast to the original, you can get any ending with all of your adherents dead, and if someone does die all you get is a few lines about how sad it makes the Haruspex feel. The way the game tracks player deaths is nicely done, but this combination just reinforces how the player is the only person who matters in the Town.

A few positives: the game has really high-quality textures and lighting, and the game balance gives you a solid survival challenge with varying accessibility options. The tincture-brewing mechanics are a huge improvement from the original. The herb collection is enjoyable, and there are a lot of great one-line NPCs (shady shop guy my beloved...). Best of all is the Fellow Traveler's character, who appears throughout the game to give exceptionally relevant conversations and advice.

However, the optimization is notoriously bad: every single outdoors asset is loaded all the time, including when you're in locations that aren't even related to them like dreams and windowless buildings! The omnipresent level fog doesn't do anything to fix this, and just cuts off your vision at an arbitrary point. Going through the entire multi-stage introduction when you start a new game is agonizing. There's also a baffling feature where wounded townsfolk will always run away from you faster than you can catch them. But the real issues are all in the narrative. Every time I think about this game, I realize it's more badly written than I thought.

The game's really only good for taking pictures in. Half of its problems are unfixable parts of the Haruspex's route, and the other half will require a huge amount of retconning to handle in the upcoming routes. It's not well written at all.

This game is so hard to rate I had trouble even knowing if I should. There is some genius hidden here: The mere concept of the game ('You have to survive hostile environments for 12 days while trying to solve a mystery') is surprisingly new and fascinating, the lore seems surprisingly deep and multi-faceted, many of the twists are legitimately interesting.

However, the vast, vast, vast majority of your time will be spent micromanaging. Micromanaging your inventory, even with upgrades, is a constant chore. Micromanaging your hunger, even the first few days, is tedious. And after the plague hits, you will also have to micromanage immunity, clean water, the condition of your clothes, having to choose long roundabout ways to avoid the plague.. And on paper that sounds great, right? Having to be on the edge of survival, having to make hard choices? Maybe, if effective micromanagement did something besides lead you to more micromanagement. You are rapidly so concerned about filling your meters that doing anything else feels dangerous. You begin having to reload constantly to find more efficient ways of playing out your day. You begin considering starting over entirely in the vague hope that more efficient use of the first days might have things go differently. You stare at the screen, realising you have spent several hours achieving literally nothing.

If this is the "intended" vision of the game designers, they have succeeded. But they have succeeded in producing a game that, instead of being an interesting look at scarcity and desperation, ends up producing nothing except frustration at the underlying mechanics. I might look at it again and change my review if the promised difficulty slider doesn't lock off content and belittle you for taking "the easy way out", though I fear that is going to be the case.
This is like playing League of Legends but least League makes sense.

This games wishes for you to suffer. I am not talking about a difficult game where you can master, mess up, and even get a bad ending; this is a game that was made for you to loathe it while playing it.

Now, on the surface, this sounds fun. After all, having the odds stacked against you and legitimately having a chance to lose is awesome. I love difficult games. However, this game is not difficult; it's a knowledge check.

If you do not wish to be spoiled, do not hover over these. However, I consider these the bare minimum you'll need to play the game and not want to shoot yourself. 

[spoiler] Hoard food, the game time speeds up. Literally, it speeds up. If you do not hoard food, you are going to starve and it's not even funny. The game moves twice as fast towards the ending. Even traveling takes multiple hours of in game time. You will not have time to get a lot of food unless you do it early. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Do the antibiotic questline for the panacea or Rubin will die no matter what. This is stupid, and simply a knowledge check from you. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hoard fingernails, do not use them early in the game. The cost will rise from one fingernail per fast travel to two. You will need a bunch of them in the late game to have a chance at good time management. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] As stated earlier, time does move faster, and it's a lot faster. Account for that in any way. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] You can get herbs by going to the south east of the map past the steppe to the steppe village. Do this in the early days or you will have a bad time. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Hoard shmowders early, do not waste them, the little girl with a bob hair cut can trade shmowders on top of the dead item shop. Trade with these people as often as you can. [/spoiler]

[spoiler] Honestly, even hoarding shmowders is only if you care enough to save the people in this game. Unlike Pathologic Classic, there is no real penalty for letting people die; you do not need to save anyone. I think that was a horrible decision since you're literally a plague doctor and it added natural difficulty in the first game, but fuck me amirite? [/spoiler]

These mechanics should not be a thing in the game. The increased time mechanic is not present in the original game and makes this game go from an extremely difficult plague sim to a gamey video game that the creators made just to mess with the players. A good example of increasing difficulty that made sense and was executed well before this is [spoiler] that individuals have lower plague resistance as the plague goes on [/spoiler] and [spoiler] In order to save a character, you must intentionally infect yourself. [/spoiler] Both of these difficulty increases appeal to the narrative and allow some type of management from the player. 

TLDR: You do not fight a plague in this game, you fight the devs. It is a big disappointment if you enjoy the early and mid game. Just play the first game.

Bad game design from a board-game style mechanism POV. It has an interesting story and setting that the devs attempted to tie into the gameplay, but they failed.

How to approach player death is a problem in most games, and one approach is to expect the player to make multiple runs, just like in any rogulike. 

IMO this fails when coupled with other genres that don't fit: base building (Don't Starve) and narrative RPG (Sunless Sea, and this game) This highlights the inherent repetition, and only works if you can enjoy the fundamentals of the game a lot. 

When you die in this game you get a permanent debuff, so you're more likely to die and get another permanent debuff...
I think the makers of this game wanted it to be about failure, to try and push through and sometimes just accept that there are limits.
Sadly, failure isn't interesting, it's just bleak nihilism and shame, and if you have any self-respect you're more likely to just bin the game.

You can tweak the difficulty settings, and the game will give you pass-agg messages saying "are you sure? you won't really be playing the true game if you do that". I find this puts me into a sort of existential crisis, where I am now somehow in charge of balancing this cursed game but without any information.  I start to question: what is difficulty? what is a fun challenge? what even is a game? 

If you want to play a game that explores the themes and consequences of failure I recommend Disco Elysium, it is done right there.
