Lets begin...... The game takes place in an "alternate reality" town during a plague, you essentially investigate the cause, try and help people and ultimately try to stop the plague all while trying to keep yourself and a handful of main characters alive throughout. The game is really difficult and I usually enjoy that (especially in survival games) but something about this just annoys the heck out of me and leaves me irritated.  You have to watch your hunger, thirst and monitor your infection level - make sure you dont catch the plague.  Food, medicine and clean water is really hard to get and becomes exponentially more so as the game goes on.  You have to CONSTANTLY ( i am not exaggerating) loot trash cans for trinkets like buttons, yarn, marbles etc and trade with NPCs for scraps of food. There are men, women, and kiddos but there are only a few preset models for each-for example, if you see 5 men in a group, 3 of them will look identical, hopefully that makes sense, I really didnt like this, ANYWAY... On top of always worrying about getting a nut or crumbs of bread to not die of starvation you have to CONSTANTLY worry about gathering enough herbs to craft under powered medicines to keep the main characters alive. You also have to maintain your gear and equipment which degrades INSANELY fast...as the plague progresses certain areas of town will be infected and there will be thugs who will attack you on sight... there are a few different weapons you can get, lets say you have a gun, you shoot a thug 2 times and you not only lost 2 bullets which are EXTREMELY expensive and rare but your revolver now lost 1/4 of its durability.  To repair it? Oh, well on top of all the other items you need but cannot get, you need to try and round up the scrap items to repair your gun/knife etc. 
You can wear special clothing in infected areas to SLOW DOWN the rate you become infected...  you wanna cut through an infected area? throw on your plague boots and take a few dozen steps and see the durability has dropped significantly...wanna repair your clothing? You know the drill, go loot for junk, try and trade with all the npcs who look identical, nobody wants what you have, rinse repeat. All while having a VERY limited inventory.  It is just too much for me personally, I didnt find this fun.  Your character WILL die multiple times but the game goes on, its actually part of the game in a way.... IDK. 

This is a "parellel universe" type situation. Its a world that looks like ours, but there is a "supernatural" force at work and the people use A LOT of lingo and terminology you will not understand and its used so often it got annoying to never understand what exactly is being said to me. Your responses also contain this weird jargon and you will not know what youre saying back to these NPCs.   

The main mission/ point to the game is essentially racing back and forth across a map to a bunch of main characters at different times and talking to them.  Quests are timed so youll never complete them all...  You get a "quest" to go see character 'A', you make your way ( at great cost) to get to this person, they are - and always will be- a stationary NPC. People in the reviews say your choices matter and will have consequences but id like to say this isnt as dramatic as you think it would or should be - in my opinion of course. Your "quests" and "decisions" are STRICTLY dialogue choices. You have a conversation that you wont understand and get more of the strange story and thats about it.  You can try and save certain main characters if they get sick, or let them die, and if certain characters die then youll lose out on some dialogue with certain characters later on but thats my point is its only dialogue..... You go to a character, you talk to them, chose dialogue options, and the convo/quest ends. Based on your dialogue options this will set up certain interactions with other stationary NPCs later on.   You dont go on missions with these characters or anything like that... Its just you talking to stationary NPCs and picking dialogue and inbetween these "interactions" you are scavenging junk to trade for junk to survive. 

I think a large part of the game for people is getting attached to the world and characters? Thats what makes all the different dialogue trees interesting for them, thats why trying to save them is fun and thats why they get so invested? Not sure... but for me its just... shallow. I dont see the magic everyone else sees.  

A thing that appealed to me in reviews  was the decay of a city while the plague takes over, but it wasnt as I thought itd be. The city is made up of a dozen or so separate "sections" or "zones".   The length of the game is 13 in game days, and on a set schedule 2 zones/ sections of the city become "infected" with the plague.  During this time if you walk through either of these 2 zones you will slowly get sick so you avoid these areas and just walk around them. Then after a day or two those 2 areas go into a "after plague" phase where a bunch of thugs wonder the streets but there is no more sickness, then after a day or two the zones recover to normal as 2 different "zones" go into plague mode.  My point is: its not like you slowly notice the sickness spreading throughout the entire city as time goes on and things completely go to hell... its just certain zones at certain times... no matter what, 80% of the city will always be normal. The plague is only in 2 sections at a time basically and it spreads at a scheduled interval.  To me that really breaks immersion.

Id say before buying this game you NEED to watch a lets play on youtube, seriously.  Its hard to explain why I find it "shallow". People will read me saying "shallow" and argue that the lore and story is super deep and theyre right (but its not interesting), im talking about the actual game play. I did find out how to cheat tho hehe.  I figureed out how to add items to my inventory, it took forever but it can be done.  Heres the problem, even with cheats the game was a drag.  I gave myself clothing you otherwise cannot get which is the "crow costume" the plague doctors wear (high plague resist), I gave myself what looks like a 98K rifle, a "wehrmacht" helmet and uniform, ammo, ENTIRE fish etc.... so I could travel anywhere and do as I pleased, shoot thugs, stay healthy... but IT WAS STILL a drag because using the rifle a few times left the damned thing broken, the clothing would degrade, id end up hungry five minutes later. Well, I dont think it worked out for me. Pathologic wants to be an interesting experiment on creating a specific dreadful experience. But it's also very much a video game. It has so many meters to keep track. And when it wants to raise tension, it just invents more meters. 

At some point, you're just not seeing the game world anymore, You're organizing your character like an excel sheet. There is so much distance between you and the game world. 

I feel like this would work better with it ditching a lot of systems, just experiencing the game world under the pressure of time and working out moral dilemmas. Focus more on that thick writing. As it is now I dont think Pathologic 2 was worth my time and I would only reccommend it to survival game fans.

Out of the hundreds of games in my library, I dont think I've ever played such a repetitive, frustrating, overhyped game in my life. All 18 hours I've spent in this game were not remotely fun or interesting, only frustrating, counter-intuitive, unbelievable and just flat out boring. I got this game on sale and still wish I could refund it.

First of all, the game is optimized terribly. I have a pretty high end computer and I still get massive frame drops just walking around the boring, cookie cutter world and every time I enter a tiny little warehouse it takes like 5 seconds to load while opening the door. My computer runs games that look twice as good and have twice the amount of resources exponentially better than this game. Also. (and this is probably the biggest issue that is making it impossible to finish the game even if I wanted to,) this game claims to have full controller support and that is simply not true. The D pad does not work in menu's, I constantly have to disconnect and re-connect my controller in-game to get it to start working again (I have never had to do this in any other games with native controller support,) and the game will not register the input of the left and right triggers or mouse buttons. Meaning I am completely unable to fight, pick locks, zoom in or out on the map, etc. After trying for hours to fix the problem on my own, I emailed Icepick customer support and politely asked them if they had any suggestions for me to try or if they could look into patching this issue, that was over a month ago and they have completely ignored me. Shoddy game, in addition to shoddy customer support.

There are countless other features of this game that are just utterly infuriating and not in any way entertaining. I love difficult games, I've played all of the From software games and love grinding away at a difficult challenge for the euphoric feeling of finally beating a difficult boss or area, this game is not like that at all. For example, you character in this game is severely diabetic (apparently.) I starved to death about 5 in game hours after I ate a loaf of bread, a fish, 2 eggs, and a glass of milk, all of which cost like 2000 dollars. Extremely unrealistic and breaks any semblance of immersion. So when I die, I am then told by the annoying theatre guy that from now on I'm going to starve to death EVEN FASTER. How fun! Also, apparently staying up all night will make you just suddenly fall over and die. Again, super unbelievable, immersion breaking, and just plain stupid and frustrating. 

The trailer for this game makes it seem like it will be way more exciting and action packed than it is. It shows basically all the most dramatic parts of the game and does not represent what the vast majority of the experience is. 95 percent of this game is just walking/running around this boring little town with identical looking buildings while listening to your character huff and puff, getting trapped in an endless amount of dead end back yards because the knee-high rock wall is to tall to step over, so that you can talk to all these boring, identical looking characters that dont even speak, just have text underneath like a skyrim mod that didnt bother to put in voice acting. All of these characters say the same cryptic, irrelevant, esoteric nonsense that feels like it was pulled straight out of a 14 year old emo kids diary or off of Jaeden Smiths twitter. "The town represents the body, and the body needs blood to survive, and the spirit is in the blood, Barakh. Therefore find the spirit of the town, and you will find its body, and your path will be illuminated etc etc." 

The audio in this game is super weird as well, not in a good way. When I am in a plague ridden area of town, you hear the same identical scream on a 4-8 second loop and it just sounds fake and again breaks any semblance of immersion which is apparently supposed to be a defining feature of this game. The soundtrack, while pretty atmospheric and eerie at first, plays over and over and over during all your hours just wandering around the map to the point of driving you nuts and wanting to turn the music volume all the way down. 

Stealth in this game is an absolute joke. It doesnt even exist. You can be in a completely empty apartment building, in an empty room with no windows, about to take 4 dollars out of a nightstand or take a dead guys organ, but somehow "they'll know" it was you who took it despite there being not a single soul around to see it. I've mentioned immersion breaking right?

I spent so many hours trying to like this game mainly because it had so many good reviews I figured I must just be looking at it the wrong way, doing something wrong, not having enough patience, not getting the point etc, so I kept trying and trying to see where the fun or any form of enjoyment or curiosity about the bland story would start to sink in, and it just got progressively more frustrating the longer I played it to the point of now having zero interest in getting any farther whatsoever in addition to not being able to complete the story with my left and right triggers and mouse buttons not working. I also cant bring myself to recommend giving your money to a studio whose customer support wont even bother answering a consumers question with a simple "sorry you're having this problem, we'll look into it" or even "we dont know how to fix it."

I wanted to like this. I really did. The story is interesting and strange. The atmosphere is intriguing. But the game play is absolutely beyond goddamn frustrating. You play as the hungriest, thirstiest human being to ever walk the planet with a mad fast metabolism. This game is essentially a "hyper-thyroid" simulator. Every waking minute of the game is spent in frustration as the developers knee cap the S*#% out of you. Can't run for more than a few seconds. In constant threat of starving to death due to your 20,000 calorie per day diet or just plain dying of thirst. Can't get food because it's mad expensive so your best bet is to trade junk for food. Guess what? That junk you just traded away for a piece of old ass bread? You needed it to fix something. Good going, idiot. Basically you play as a doctor who wanders around town starving to death and digging through trash cans and that's no joke. I wish I could say I was just being a salty, sarcastic jerk but that really is what the game play loop is. That is until your health gets so low that you get stuck in a death loop where you die, get resurrected, and then die again 3 seconds later because you always respawn with the same level of health you had when you died. Who the f^%$ thought that was a good idea? Also, every time you die you continue the game with a new handicap as punishment. As if repsawning with no f@*#ing health wasn't punishment enough. I made it to the fourth day. I really want to finish this game. I actually really like it but the difficulty level is through the roof. It needs to be brought down a notch so that you can actually accomplish missions without non stop panic of starving to death or dying of lack of sleep. 

TLDR: Very cool game that is ruined by idiotic game mechanics. Don't waste your time.

EDIT: Due to the game stressing that death comes with permanent added handicaps I didn't realize I could reload earlier saves to get out of the death loop. So that's a plus. Also didn't realize they had added sliders to customize the difficulty level to make it less frustrating. So there is some hope if you find the game to be infuriating. I still wouldn't recommend it to just anyone however. This is for a certain kind of person. I can see why it has a cult following. It is appealing and interesting. Especially if you were there when it first came out and you remember it from way back then. The same way I'd say Deus Ex is incredible but probably would not recommend it to just anyone. Is it good? Yes. Would everyone today feel the same way I did back when I first played it? No. It's janky and I didn't notice or care back then. This game falls into that kind of category.

The game starts off throwing you pretty blind into the deep-end of a lot of lore you just will not understand starting the game. Difficulty is also kinda hit and miss, the primary difficulty is honestly more "annoyance" than actual difficulty, Is combat hard? No, you're generally far more capable than any of the enemies you run into, weapons really only being required if your outnumbered though your strongest asset is honestly just being faster than everyone else. There are very few enemies you are actually required to fight and you'll generally find yourself running past everyone as using virtually any weapon is either too costly, or leaves it in a broken state, usually both; which is fine because as long as your not trying to fist fight armed soldiers who are everywhere and (Almost) always allied with you can generally beat anyone in a 1 on 1 to 1 on 2 fight without damage with your bare hands or quickly peel them off with a nearby guard. You will still usually choose just to run past everyone however as again, you're considerably faster, and its usually not worth the time or effort to do any of the fighting yourself.

Further annoyance is found in the weapons/apparel repairs and keeping fed/hydrated. Most gear breaks near instantly and trading for the scraps to repair anything is again, usually more time and annoyance than what its worth and you'll generally just choose to survive off whatever equipment you pass by which is mostly adequate. As for food and water you are literally the thirstiest and hungriest person on the planet, especially near the end game where about 10 seconds of running around requires your thirst being topped off or your max energy is damaged. Even if you have a good stockpile on hand the sheer number of times you need to break away from the game just to decide what to eat or drink is again annoying.

Now if you want to keep everyone alive... good luck, this is actually difficult, and possibly impossible as it seems some people are just scripted to die regardless of what you do. For those that aren't, you're medicines are highly ineffective aside from the sparse "miracles" which are guaranteed cures. Otherwise your fighting an RNG roll which is usually weighted against you. This could be more tense if honestly even half of the characters were likable but aside from a select few they just aren't (don't worry they usually don't like you either) you at best take care of them out respect for the idea that its your job than any actual desire for them to live; which again it seems to matter very little who is alive at the end anyway.

Pathologic 2 is almost one of the richest and most interesting games I have ever played.
My experience playing the first few days was exactly what I never knew I wanted from an RPG. Days 1-6 felt like they stood on the edge of a knife. Constantly about to die from one thing or another, making tough decisions about what to do with my limited time and resources. Feeling like I would fall irreparably behind if I didn't work to understand every bit of information and game system. Utterly engrossing.
At some point I got the plague while scavenging a house on the brink of starving to death but I was sure I was nearly done making a cure. This was a prank so I spent hours and hours of game time completely locked in, making sure no opportunity slipped through my fingers, still barely clinging on. After investing the last of my borrowed time in making another prototype cure, my stomach and inventory were empty, my health was low and finding another sick person to serve as guinea pig would definitely kill me. I had no choice but to drink it myself, fully expecting it to give me some new horrible status condition and effectively soft-lock my current save. When instead I saw the infection bar recede and fully vanish I jumped out of my chair.
I wish I had stopped playing there though. I had a number of technical issues with the game. Framerate slowing to ~10 every 3 seconds even on min settings, several bugged out NPC interactions that obscured some of the later plot developments. One catastrophic bug occurred after getting fast traveled to the cathedral to meet with someone. That NPC spoke ominously about something about to happen, so I thought it was another world upending twist of the Pathologic knife when after this conversation every NPC appeared to have dialogue when I looked at them with my special eyes but then wouldn't talk to me. Curse of silence maybe? I wondered for HOURS how I was supposed to make any headway on understanding this ailment before googling out of frustration and realizing that it was a bug. And now I was going to have to load a save from the night before. After my first death the load screen told me I had 6 deaths, which at first I thought that was a really cool odd-ball story telling element that was going to be explained in one of the fourth wall breaking moments. Just a bug, which I only realized after finishing the game and trying to google its explanation.
More broadly though, even without those bugs I would not recommend you play the game. Not the whole thing anyway. The story starts to choke on itself in the second half. The characters of the town, who present so much intrigue on the first few days, are not that interesting on second inspection. They're all very well characterized, mostly as snooty and annoying, looking down on steppe-son Artemy and forcing you to toil in the gutter. But they're also completely useless. Even later characters who are made out to be powerful, imposing threats never do anything but stand there. Important people's houses are all weirdly partitioned so their state only effects a single self-contained zone. You start to feel like you're the only real thing alive in this paper-doll pantomime world. Ohhh man that was all intentional wasn't it; that's what the meta narrative was talking about the whole time! I wish it hadn't been. Maybe this kind of eyebrow waggling scanned a lot better around the release of the first game but once I started to see through the NPCs the world felt hollowed out and I was not interested in playing with the paper dolls for another 14 hours. I think the story had heart and I wish it had been told straight. I just couldn't give a shit about anything after reading pompous witty philosophy one-liner #298 from idle lip-flapper #12 who, from a gameplay perspective, has 0 impact on the world. Those guys in whiteface don't get any philosophy books to read from but at least the had the guts to kick my ass. Should have made them the central antagonists.
By day 9 I was fully divested and should have quit again. I stubbornly stuck with it and eventually got the good ending where all of the characters get stuck to popsicle sticks and parade through the town singing "Its a Small World". The end had some nice moments that should have made me feel something. I even thought some of the "n'est pas une conversation" conversations at the end were well written and thought provoking.

This could have been the best game of all time. Have you played Outer Wilds? If you haven't you should give it a look.

Pathologic 2 had the potential to be an outstanding hidden gem but in the end, it suffers from the same bloody fate as many other brilliant games out there: [b]f*cking terrible devs doing an utterly bad job in order to delive a pinch more of challenge so they're able to brag about their game being difficult (even if the cost is ruining it entirely), forgetting to test their own game and squash bugs instead of adding more useless dialog throughout the empty town you find yourself in.[/b]

Pathologic itself is complex, unforgiving if playing as intended, mind twisting, narrative-driven feturing an ocean of text and strange language, and 100% psychological horror. You will get lost many times, lose opportunities many times, but after all you realize that's the catch.
And that's fine. It is supposed to be difficult. The set up prepares you for a miserable experience since the very beginning, and it warns a dozen times you are to get the grip of things instead of being led by the hand.

HOWEVER, as no game is perfect, you find out soon that Pathologic 2 has some game-killing, deadly serious defective systems:

1. Basic needs. While the whole world feels unnatural but somehow very realistic at the same time (put aside the lack of character model diversity), basic needs are very very very very poorly handled, tearing down immersion. Artemy needs to eat barrells of food per day and drink gallons of water if he is to not die while sleeping - which can absolutely happen - and the food is UNGODLY expensive. I mean, yeah, the town is facing a huge shortage of many products but that's not possibly an excuse. You struggle to make 1k coins, then you find out a fish that heals a laughable amount of hunger [b]and recovers no health at all[/b] costs you nearly 700 coins.
As one would expect, jumping and running consumes stamina by a lot, bringing even more variables to mess with need meters. Turns up to be awful as hell when we barely have enough daytime to explore and uncover the world around us, summed with the f*cked up mindless economy system they implemented here.

2. [b]Death. Dying DOES NOT take away even 1% of your exhaustion (not to be confused with stamina), leading to scenarios where you can be HARD LOCKED WITHIN A DEATH LOOP if you have no healing items in your inventory. I guess it is just too hard for russians to use their brains and acknowledge the fact that when you move a respawning character back to the last saving point while giving a random death penalty but no chance to heal, no chance to search for items or sleep (you can't sleep in any bed/bedroll/couch you find) WITH NO PREVIOUS WARNING ABOUT IT, you frustrate them. Would be better to make it permadeath and clarify the real importance of dealing with exhaustion above all.
I've been gaming since '97 and I can't really remember a game that failed so miserably in the SIMPLEST MISSION that is respawning a character.[/b]

3. Performance issues. Notorious and gross. Devs say recommended settings are a 16GB RAM rig with NVIDIA GeForce GTX 970 plus an intermediate 3GHz processor but mind you: even far more powerful PC owners reported stutterings and issues that shouldn't happen. Yes it is a beautiful and demanding game indeed, but f*cking ugly optimized.
If you face crashes, textures not rendering correctly and less than 50fps with even minimum requirements, check out forums on how to fix those by changing params directly inside Pathologic 2 files.

4. Bugs. You won't immerse yourself in a town where you fight a spreading plague; you will be fighting [b]all unsolved bugs devs were too lazy to NOT MESS WITH during this REMAKE.[/b] I mean yeah, let's make a remake, but let's not touch any glitch, bug or whatever.
I promptly lost interest in Pathologic 2 due to 2 unnaceptable bugs for a game like this where loading a previous game does not erase your death (yeah I know it is laughable but, remember: russian devs. They have no clue): first was a guy teleporting right behind my back and stabbing me to death in a single hit while I had half HP left as soon as I opened a random door. Second was a guy crossing a prop barrier a.k.a invisible wall when I was chasing him.

Devs made the impossible true: failing miserably at a game that is 95% talking to people, trading, walking, collecting herbs and fast travelling. If I bought my 7yo son an Unity license he would come up with a better game, like everyone else around here could.

If you still want to play this overpriced garbage, then read about how every core mechanic works and avoid playing vanilla Imago difficulty. There's a mod that do what devs apparently couldn't (aside from being humans with more than 10 IQ), fixing game balance by a bit.

[h1] Pathologic 2 [/h1]
     Pathologic 2 theoretically had a lot to offer, a Plague themed RPG with focus on the story and character development with good writing and a challenging gameplay, fitting for a real plague story. That said, it has accomplished some of the things I thought it would, while not being able, in my opinion of course, to reliably accomplish some other stuff.

     [b] Story [/b] -> Review of the main points of the storytelling, no major spoilers included
     This for me has been what pulled me through 20 hours of the game, the characters are engaging and feel real enough, including the main character which has an interesting backstory and placement in the world. The antagonists don't follow a manichaeistic logic, usually, but not always, falling into gray areas of morality, which also helps the storytelling and the overall feel of the world. Another thing is how the game world tells a story by itself, serving also as a character in the story, the game tells you the town is structured like a living being, and it feels like it most of the time, with each part of the town having its own characteristics and function, much like organs in an organism, this for me is also one of the main points of the story, because the allegory of the living city has always been an interesting storytelling and literary strategy that makes the setting that much more interesting and real.

     [b] Gameplay [/b]
     This is why I will not be playing Pathologic 2 in its entirety, the gameplay loop is boring, maybe one of the most boring 20 hours I've played in a game. It consists basically of gathering herbs, bartering essential items with random NPCs, walking around the city, a fairly basic and cheesy combat system that has no depth to it, an interesting gameplay mechanic which is the diagnostic and treatment of people affected or vulnerable to the plague, a pretty interesting and innovative mechanic to a RPG but that is shadowed by the other 85% of the tedious gameplay and an annoying survival based physiology system to the character, which is your biggest threat, the difficulty from the game comes from min/maxing your hunger which will lead you to hours of scavenging and bartering with no real sense of reward when you fulfill it. 

     [b] Graphics, Art and Audiovisual presentation [/b]
     For a 2019 game, it's pretty bogged down, it probably won't get in your way while playing, but not once I had a "wow" moment while playing it, with most of what is presented graphically being pretty forgettable aside from specific scenes. The art is consistent, has a good feel for the story it's illustrating and is one of the pros of the game. The audio and sound effects are creepy, if a bit repetitive, but of good quality, it serves the game well and fits well with the more creepy moments of the game, but the sound effects of the herbs are a bit annoying in my opinion, but I think that is by design, to give the audio part in the gameplay also.

     I can't say I didn't enjoy the game at all, the storytelling is enjoyable, but with the gameplay as it stands, I would not have bought the game. I wish that in the future we can have a game with a good low fantasy dark world set in a plague, that has a great storytelling AND a compelling gameplay, but Pathologic 2 has not been it for me. Even so, I think they, the writers and developers, have created an interesting world, with interesting medicine themed mechanics and would wish to see more from them.

[h1]INITIAL STEAM REVIEW (5/6/2019)[/h1]
First things first:

- Get it only if you know what you'll be dealing with.
- I'd recommend the 1st game over this one.

Pathologic 2 does many things right but makes some mistakes that the first game didn't, 14 years ago.

It's ironic how the original game felt esoteric and cryptic due to its story and narrative, whereas Pathologic 2 tries not to ostracize players from its world by hinting a bit too much at the greater picture (even the death mechanic could be considered sort of a  giveaway) and inevitably does so with its unrefined mechanics, while it should be the other way around.

Example of balanced system -> Infection :
In Pathologic: easy to get infected, antibiotics are largely available
In Pathologogic 2: not that easy to get infected as long as you have even a bit of immunity left, less antibiotics to be found.

Example of unbalanced system -> Exhaustion:
In Pathologic: exhaustion gauge is full after ~ 10 hours, you can stock 3-4 coffee beans and 1 lemon a day without having to scour the whole town
In Pathologic 2: bar fills faster, lemons and especially coffee are not that easy to procure.

Pathologic 2 is a weird and unique experience, but at its current state it is besmeared by optimization and balance issues. Its narrative, story and atmosphere are suffocating under the weight of its mechanics and I’m pretty sure that heavy reliance on meta-gaming to avoid hitting a roadblock wasn’t something its creators intended.

I'm waiting for the performance and difficulty customization patch and  I'd be happy to give the game a thumbs up if said issues are mended.

You know the scene in Indiana Jones where he barely slides through the closing rock door, and realizes he forgot his hat? He reaches in with just enough time to grab his hat and not have his arm crushed. Playing Pathologic is like that, except the Mr.Jones forgot the Idol too. He has to run all the way back inside the tomb, past the boulder, grab the idol, run back to the sliding door and still somehow manage to squeeze underneath before it shuts. And if he gets crushed on the way back out; it's not game over. Jones is expected to continue the movie despite his fatal wounds.

You will never have enough time or knowledge to play Pathologic with any level of success on your first try. In that sense, I view the game as a time-loop style game. A time loop that lasts upwards of 14 real hours, in which you will need to have your route perfectly planned for each of the game's 12 days. Failure to meet the harsh deadlines imposed upon you along the way means you can be locked out of important story beats, and whats more; cause the death of practically any living NPC. If you don't have prerequisite knowledge about the game, you will suffocate under the enormous amount of vague dialogue, terrible combat, time-sensitive events, and hunger/thirst/sickness survival bars.

I suffocated, and there wasn't much fun to be had before that point. I've learned since quitting the game that the game's difficulty settings are likely the cause of most of my gripes; with the setting "Intended Difficulty" being the hardest difficulty, and is well beyond the point realistically expecting the player would succeed without the help of a guide, or several failed playthroughs. Had I known that practically everyone advises against "Intended" mode on their first playthough, I might have continued playing Pathologic, but I certainly will not be rewinding all the way to day 1 just to do it all over again with a slower hunger meter. I mourn for what this game may have been for me otherwise as many of it's aspects are genuinely brilliant.

I cannot think of a single type of person who I know for sure would love Pathologic, but those people are out there. Sadly, Steam's 2hr refund policy will be worthless to you should you attempt to try before you buy, as the introductory first day will take at least that before you get into the meat of the game.

This game is different from any other game I played before. However, different doesn't always mean good. It's fine, if you use mods/in-game sliders/cheats whatever. Otherwise, it's a very negative experience. I tried many of the so-called "hardcore" games, ranging from survival action to stealth tactics. Store page says "a groundbreaking open-world horror RPG". Groundbreaking in what way? Was there supposed to be a bug, where is the ground breaks? If it's true, then yes, it's a groundbreaking game. 
Horror? Not really. What you should actually fear are lack of autosave and terrible combat system. 
RPG? You have needs, you can wear clothes. Your dialogue choices have very low impact on the story. It doesn't matter what you will do at all. Save people or don't. Kill everyone or play passively. 

I like the "atmosphere" of the game, but there are many problems that I mentioned and few more. So in short, here's the deal.

[h1]Terrible combat system[/h1]

1.1. Hiboxes are the worst I saw. You can punch the enemy early, and your hit will be registered. 
1.2. Some enemy attacks ignore blocks. It can be a serious problem when you fight the worms/odonghs, since they break your blocks often, and they hit like tanks. You can handle one, more or less, but few is a problem.
1.3. Weapons malfunction all the damn time. For this reason, ranged weapons are a very unreliable option. 
1.4 Equipment has durability. Few attacks with scalpel can break it (you also need it for autopsy, which also breaks it). Clothes break fast, either from combat related damage or the plague "air". Guns can break after few shots. This is a very primitive way to introduce a durability mechanic. It should have been smarter/more complex or none at all. 

Combat is not mandatory, but as time passes, you will encounter more and more bandits on the streets. Groups with knives etc.

[h1]No time left[/h1]

Your needs will decrease very fast. I understand that devs wanted us to fight for survival, but the time amount of time you spend walking from one location to another, plus the speed at which your needs drop, is a bad combination. You are trying are spending hours to visit the same characters, getting ingredients for cure, and to heal them, just to find out in the end, that all of this is not important. 

[h1]Niche game[/h1]

1. Characters have very few voiced lines. No matter, main or side character. They say one phrase and the rest is a text-based dialogue. 
2. I had a bug when I couldn't interact with NPC. Full game reboot helped. Once, guards blocked the door in a house and I had to kill them.
3. Devs added sliders that you can tweak, but these are just numbers. How am I, as a player, supposed to know which numbers are good? After playing, it once, maybe. That requires you to actually complete it.
4. Two of three campaigns/characters are still not available. Yeah, small team and so on. The problem here is that three years passed, and they still haven't released at least Bachelor story. 

[h1]Final[/h1]

Until they fix the combat, bugs, rework/remove durability, change the rate of character needs to drop and release at least one more campaign, I can't recommend this game. There's a reason why it failed commercially.

I did not start playing this series on Pathologic 1, and I'm not the type to shy away from a difficult game at all. But this game left a sour taste in my mouth, the cryptic and uninteresting dialogue, gratuitous and unnecessary female nudity and bulging nipples, and strange fever dream scenes that just pointlessly plopped down executor and giant bull assets. I don't know much about Eurasian folklore or culture, but I think that shit needed to be toned down, it really would have decreased the file size and the amount of work that devs would have to put into the game. Very strange game design direction overall.

The game also does a really terrible job at giving you feedback for starvation and sleep deprivation. I can still run around the town, up and down side to side, while dying of starvation and lack of sleep. How on earth am I still able to do these things while starving and tired? How was this an oversight in a survival game? I ended up being as reckless as possible with hunger and sleep so that I could get a couple more objectives done. And for what? Just so the game can get harder as I died from hunger and illness attempting to complete an objective. 

On a positive note, the sound design for ambient sounds was phenomenal, kept me on edge and pushed my face in the dirt and dragged me along with how eerie and oppressive it was. 

I really regret buying this game and giving it a long and honest try, because now I cannot refund it.

The game's performance, especially on PC, is a technical nightmare. I recommend using an RTX card or higher-end GPU, such as the ASUS TUF Gaming series, paired with ample SSD storage and RAM. Even with this hardware, you might still experience frame rate drops and other performance hiccups, likely due to poor optimization. You'll find yourself slowing down to a comical pace, as if channeling your inner Jim Carrey, while the other characters stare in bewilderment.

While Pathologic 2 aims to improve upon its predecessor, it falls short in several areas. The elongated gameplay, filled with excessive walking, can feel tedious and artificial. Character models, though detailed, often appear stiff and unnatural, hindering emotional connection. 

The game's world-building, while intriguing, lacks the subtlety and mystery of the original. The over-reliance on overt symbolism and exposition diminishes the impact of the narrative. The music, a crucial element in the first game, is noticeably weaker in the sequel. It seems the budget was allocated elsewhere, perhaps towards those fancy Kickstarter masks.

Unlike the original, which offered three distinct storylines, Pathologic 2 limits you to a single, linear narrative with 4 endings (although with only one true ending I guess it all doesn't really matter). While the game presents choices, the outcome is often predetermined, leaving players feeling constrained. The emphasis on survival mechanics, such as scavenging and trading, can be both engaging and frustrating, depending on your playstyle.

Conclusion: A Cautionary Tale

Pathologic 2 is a flawed game with significant performance issues and questionable design choices. While it offers some improvements over the original, it ultimately fails to capture the magic of its predecessor. I would advise caution to potential players and suggest exploring the original Pathologic for a more rewarding experience.

The original game, despite its quirks like the tiny mugger that would run screaming at you to the front door like a woman half dressed with a robe, offered more engaging and challenging combat. It was a bolder, more ambitious vision that didn't shy away from its unique aesthetic and challenging gameplay.

The game's easier accessibility, thanks to the rearranged locations, might be a boon for the Surgeon character. The plague's confinement to the town and the convenient distance to the medical shop and pub reduce the need for combat. However, the game's mechanics, like the risk of having items stolen from your home, can be frustrating. It's a strange design choice that forces players to micromanage their inventory, turning them into pack mules.

It seems the true intention here is to set the stage for future games in the series, leaving us to wonder if the true magic of Pathologic has been lost. If you're considering playing this game, I suggest you stock up on water and patience. And remember, a game is only as good as its execution, no matter how grand the vision.

Well, the game certainly keeps you thinking long after you finished it, you gotta give it that. It is interesting and unique in concept, after all. Pathologic 2 is a pretty alright game. It's not fun, though - which, realistically, is part of the point in the experience. However, I personally find the features irritating rather than interesting. To begin with...

Survival Meters. The survival meters are implemented better than many other games, because rather than being strange, obligatory things that you are forced to take care of in situations that seem random or outright ridiculous, it makes sense that your character, under the duress of a plague and running around all day, would likely need a lot of food, water, and rest. However, they're still the irritating, fast-rising meters that take a lot away from my enjoyment of the game. Maybe it's a personal taste issue, but in almost every game with these garish meters, they rarely make any logical sense with how fast they rise, how much you have to eat just to be "fine", ect. I know that part of the game's story is about coping with starvation, dehydration, lacking money, and simply getting sick; but, honestly? I feel like it's more of an excuse for poor game design.

The game's story and "mood" are interesting, if a bit...over-bearing. I have this problem with some games and media, especially recently - there is simply an overbearing feeling of total dread and pointlessness. Again this could simply be my preferences, but I don't think any story is all that interesting when it's simply a conga line of trauma, death, and despair. Even if it ends with a light at the end of the tunnel, at that point I couldn't care less because the entire journey felt useless.

The way that the game is set up to purposefully stress you so you have to run/walk across the city every five minutes becomes more of an exercise in patience than anything, at a certain point I stopped caring about many of the things to do because the game seems to want to make a point about how you can't save everyone, you can't do everything, you can't always be the good guy, and other very critical (if realistic) viewpoints. That's all well and good, but, I just can't bring myself to *care* about the messages when the game makes it possible to do many of those things, but only if you're willing to tear your hair out and min-max.

The saving system is...annoying. I never personally liked saving systems where you had to run up to some random object just to smack it and sprint the other way, especially in an open-world game. I can abide it in certain games because it feels less intrusive, but not here, personally.

The infection system isn't really...interesting? It feels, again, as if it's more simply designed to be obtuse and frustrating to deal with; which, if it was, fair enough! However, given that it's another one the imperfect "survival bars", it simply makes me roll my eyes and reload a save because the game cheekily decides to spawn a cloud of death directly in front of me, or randomly chooses to have opening a random door give me sickness. Obviously that might be the point, but, it again feels like an excuse.

All in all, the entire game seems like it's *fine*, but I can't help but not want to really play it anymore. It's not because I don't think I can, or because it's not fun (it's not necessarily supposed to be fun), but the entire experience feels empty to me. Sure, the story and characters are well written, but when everything surrounding them feels so jagged and awkward to handle on top of having mechanics that kick you in the teeth repeatedly, I just don't think it's worth playing - the experience reminds me that I have actual work to do and honestly, promises that it's probably a better idea to do that instead. Discussing, maybe watching? Perhaps. Playing? I'd rather pass.

This game's core design revolves around timers. Timers, if used sparingly, can add to tension. When abused to this degree, though, it destroys the gameplay. There are 5 timers going at any given time (Hunger, Thirst/Stamina, Infection/Immunity, Exhaustion, and Health), and at the base setting, the aggression of the timers is infuriating. If you want to experience this world at a semi-enjoyable pace, do yourself a favor and set all the bars to their most forgiving setting. It is set up to be a multi-playthrough game, but with probably more than 20 hours of dialogue menus and 10 hours of sprinting around for fetch quests and trying to barter for resources, why would anyone want to go through this a second time?

I picked this up on sale, and I have to say, I still don't feel it was worth it. Unforgiving game design can add tension under the right circumstances, but overdone it can ruin a game. Multiple timers, constant backtracking, constant fetch quests, and hours of text dialogue are not good game design - they are a lazy attempt to add length and tension rather than coming up with more interesting design and allowing visual world-building to show how dire the situation is. The world is beautiful and the atmosphere is great, but you will have no time to stop and take it in. You will eat multiple times per day while still starving to death. You will run all the way across the map to receive a quest all the way at the other end of the map, then you'll die of hunger or exhaustion because you didn't spend half the day trying to barter with the locals. The game is nearly unplayable even lowering all the difficulty sliders to their easiest position, and every time you die you not only lose maximum health (across every save you would attempt to load) but also your survival meters remain where they were when you died - so if you died of hunger, guess what? You're still hungry but now have lower health. I could forgive almost all of this if you didn't spend so much time in dialogue menus, because then when you load your save you have to go back to sprinting across the map to click through the same laborious dialogue menus. An excellent world, a brilliant idea, and a beautiful premise executed in the most egregious and unplayable way possible. Spend your hard-earned money on something else. I'd get a refund, but I spent so much time in dialogue menus I missed the refund window.

First of all, let it be known i have not finished the game. I plan to and will, as i am sure the ending is worth it. The game is extremely unique, to the point i can confidently say i have never played anything similar. The atmosphere is brilliant, the story is great, the choice system is i think revolutionary and the way said choices are brought forth is very inteligent. Then why the negative review...two reasons:

First: I have backed this game when the project was announced back in 2014 i think, as i could already see the potential it held. and while news were scarce, the occasional email with an update on progress was always refreshing. and now 5 years down the line...the game doesnt run very well. the game is not big in term of ressources used, the graphics are fine but simple and the map is far from enormous, yet it barely scratched 60fps for me, and i know a lot of users are having worse performance. Also the game has the annoying tendency to crash in the middle of gameplay, like that, for no reason. When you know progress can only be saved at specific spots, this becomes frustrating really fast.

Second: Death...i have no problem with dying .. when its my fault, didnt eat >> starved, didnt rest >> collapses, ignore the plague >> dies of sickness. this is fair enough. The game has a mechanic where all your death are counted, even if you restore a previous save, and the game make it really clear that dying is NOT good on the long run. The main problem is that the combat system is so garbage you WILL die because of it, no matter how well equipped you are due to a few key points. Ennemies do not make noises, apart from occasional grunts on hit, they do not make noise, especially footsteps. I ahve died twice after engaging an ennemy and getting stabbed in the back by another who had sprinted behind me like a ninja. The stamina management is a disgraceful failure, the rate at which you lose max stamina is insane. sprinting for ten seconds with a full bar will make you lose 10% of it, and as soon as you start throwing punches it dives. trying to take on more than one guy in close combat is a nightmare as them hitting your guard cost stamina, and thus you cant attack, and they keep attacking, effectively stunlocking you. Running is not an option as they have infinite stamina. and the last nail in the coffin: if you get hit, your character will get all dizzy, spinning around like a drunkard, but they can tank uppercuts without flinching.
I can already hear the smartass guild telling me to use a gun, great idea, ammo management is difficult, but this is fine, i dont expect a village lost in the sticks to be sitting on crates of ammo, but in that case, make the bullet counts... even a headshot will not kill a guy, a guy who is sick with the plague to boot. And back to the previous point, hitting them with a bullet will barely make them flinch. Cherry on the cake, the revolver jams extremely often, even in near perfect condition.

So in short, great story, excellent story telling, garbage combat, i know it is not the main point of the game, but it is not avoidable. you HAVE to fight at some point. And the system is so simple it's incredible they managed to make it so bad, especially in this day and age where everybody before you has made such mistakes and you simply have to look at them to know what NOT to do.

PS: as mentionned before, i backed the game at the beginning, which normally entitles me to a free copy of the game on release...i never received it, one more reason to be disapointed.

The game made by people that don't really understand games.

It offers a high level of challenge, but never any respite, any reward for it. Knowing that certain things can happen without you is great; the lack of control is great since Pathologic is effectively a horror game, but this game doesn't understand contrast. Instead of feeling like you're bravely pushing through against bad odds, you end up trying to outsmart the game itself and its systems.

Some people will defend this, saying that challenge is great. And I agree, I like challenging games. However, if you find yourself quickloading dozens of times to replay a specific day because you keep failing miserably because of things completely outside of your control, there's a problem with the game's design.

Pathologic actively dissuades you from exploring its world or experimenting at all. If you ever ask yourself if you should go help an NPC, explore a new location, try robbing a house, or fight a bandit, the answer is almost always "no." Whatever you do, you almost never get anything useful out of it and only waste precious time (which means more hunger, less health and stamina). There's basically no risk/reward, only dumb luck and a lot of fast running.

Is this suffering worth it? I don't think so.

First, the gameplay isn't better than it was in the original. 90% of the time you'll just be an errand boy. The combat is janky and neither fun, nor engaging, and, like many other things, is rarely even worth getting into: the few weapons you have wear out very quickly, and the repair costs are so ridiculously high that you can basically view them as disposable tools. In the original, with some luck and skill you could battle the bandits at night, even make a bit of money off that, and repairing equipment wasn't such a huge problem, but forget all of that here.

Second, the story. I could stand the gameplay issues if the game was well-written... But it's not!

It seems that tons of people are absolutely enamored with Pathologic 2's writing, but if you've played the original, you'll likely agree it's incomparable. The original Pathologic was subtle, elegant, thought-provoking and philosophical. The game tried to make you feel things and think about things. In contrast, the writing of Pathologic 2 is basically, "You're such a moron! You know nothing about anything, and you're going to fail miserably in everything!" repeated over and over in different voices. The game tries to be mysterious and to make you feel like you're fighting Death itself, but all it does is belittle you and speak in riddles, which gets old pretty fast.

It's funny that Marble Nest, a mini chapter that served as a demo for the game, was a much more complete and well-rounded experience.

And on top of all that... THE GAME IS INCOMPLETE.  And I don't think it'll ever be complete, because Ice-Pick Lodge doesn't understand how game development works. They failed all deadlines, they failed their supporters and they couldn't even fulfill their promises to the backers. Physical prizes? Not received. Digital goodies? Laughable. (Imagine that one of the digital goodies for the backers was one regular item that you can simply make in the game, with no special effects whatsoever. Can you imagine being a Skyrim backer and receiving a single dragon bone for that?)

My verdict: you're better off playing the original.

This game has great potential. It's original, it's provocative, it's surreal. It talks in whispers about life and death. It makes you struggle, get despaired, hopeful - and despaired again. It raises hard questions - whom to save, whether to be "good", what is it to be "good" - so you'll have to make hard choices. It's here not to merely entertain you - it has a more ambitious goal.

However, for me this game failed to live up to its ambitions.

There are 12 days in total. The first 4 to 5 days are great at setting up the atmosphere, characters and mysteries. The mechanics of survival is very challenging but it feels authentic and fair - and fulfilling to overcome. The music, the design, the unsettling world left such a great impression on me that I, without any hesitation, put Pathologic in my personal "top 10 best games ever".

However, next days do not bring almost anything new to the table. The mechanics of survival doesn't change much. It keeps being challenging though - even more so if you didn't excel at gathering right resources in the beginning. A few times I ended up in an absurdly tough spot, where I had to repeat a sequence of actions over and over again till I got it just right to survive. Hello my old friend, Dark Souls. You can reduce difficulty, which I didn't as, well, I trusted the developers: the hardest difficulty is the recommended one.

The characters and mysteries didn't really pay off for me. When the game is great at making plot setups, the stories and characters often lack any meaningful development. While there are some interesting ideas and twists, overall the story doesn't feel complete. Also, while the game makes the point that to solve the mysteries, the player must think for himself rather than follow markers on the map, almost all of the quests are solved exactly by running from one marker to another.

I'll still be waiting for the next part though. Hopefully, the bold and brilliant ideas of Pathologic will get a better execution.
